notes.urn:cts:latinLit:stoa0114a.stoa004.opp-l: Several scanning errors corrected silently (e.g. 'patens' for 'potens', 'cam' for 'cum', 'eat' for 'est'). Uncertain readings: 'pudor(i amor)is' follows the bracketed restoration; 'umore maria. turgescit' taken as 'umore maritata turgescit'; 'nouelli. praesegminis' taken as young shoots/buds; 'i* te libram' read as 'in te libram'; 'paris fecti' is corrupt (perhaps 'parricidii' or similar) and is rendered loosely as '[committing] a crime'; 'fractura procellarum' rendered literally, though the sense (the calm after storms) is unclear; 'ruentum' read as 'ruentium'. The 'second captivity' in the Roman church apparently refers to the Symmachan–Laurentian schism and its synods.

Line 3 heading: 'V. S.' read as vir spectabilis. Line 4: 'Victor' and 'Maximus' puns on names are implicit. Line 6: John is called both 'prophet and apostle', apparently conflating John the Baptist (born to Zacharias) with John the Apostle; translated as given. The phrase 'ab uniuersis\' iura- ereditur Iohannes apostolus clauis. esse uerborum' is garbled by scanning; read as 'ab uniuersis iure creditur Iohannes apostolus clauis esse uerborum'. 'senior gratia quam natura' rendered 'grace was older than nature'. In line 2 'semiuiuis palpitantia motibus' and 'quicquid portio sinistra' are rendered literally; the latter's sense is uncertain.

5.1: 'caltam' is unclear (perhaps for 'laudem' or 'cautam'); rendered as 'esteem' by sense. 'monitorem.. torem' is a dittography. 5.2: read 'nouam' for 'nonam', 'conuersationis' for 'couersationis'; the sentence 'dei nostri extitit lex uoluntas omnis dispensatio...' is loosely punctuated in the edition. 5.3: 'dum testes sui arbiter se uociferatur' seems corrupt (perhaps 'teste te ... arbitro'); read 'clementior' for 'dementior'. 6.1: read 'uana' for 'nana', 'ut' for 'at'; 'diro diaboli a sententia sua motus imperio' taken as 'moved from his judgement'. 7.1: read 'origini' for 'origin', 'suo effectu' (?) for 'suffectu', 'hebetatur' for 'hebetater'.

8.ab1: 'V. S.' taken as 'vir spectabilis'. 8.2: 'fibula' read as 'fibra' (fibre); 'nastiter exercitu' is corrupt, translated as 'nascitur exercitio'; 'auara sunt nota diligentum' is obscure (perhaps 'vota diligentium', 'the wishes of those who love are greedy'); 'Gregorium' presumably Gregory of Nazianzus. 9.1: 'Bosphorum' among constellations is odd (perhaps Bootes); 'est est' is a dittography; 'ia me' read as 'in me'; a stray '15' (line number) omitted; 'debuit tibi macte et mea orationem professio' is corrupt, translated by sense as 'my profession too owed you, blessed one, a speech'; 'legi quia' is uncertain, rendered 'Know that'.

9.2: ‘classico meo’ is taken as a personal name (Classicus); it could instead be a common noun, and the sentence ‘mihi classicus non meretur imperiis, quicquid non inponit obsequio’ is obscure. ‘Degenerare sublimiter’ is an oxymoron: to depart from his ancestry by surpassing it. 10.1: ‘uictem, nisi exercerentur terga, mortalibus non praeberent artis est’ is corrupt or lacunose (probably a sentence about oxen or animals and food, then ‘artis est, quod...’); marked [...]. 11.1: ‘nauta puppibus’ repeats ‘puppibus’ and seems corrupt (a verb such as ‘sulcat’ or ‘transit’ appears to be lost); ‘insinuandum orbitatis miseratio’ is likely corrupt (perhaps ‘insinuat’); ‘prout eius tribuunt’ lacks a subject, perhaps ‘merita’; ‘oris ... iubar’ is rendered ‘radiance of eloquence’. Scanning errors corrected: Proseoutionem, Arateris, defmdabo, Eusebins, plenitude, deeus.

In the Narration: 'accepts' read as accepta; 'nos triticeam' read as uos; 'nestram' read as uestram; 'cam' read as cum. 'non mutare quod nonum' is evidently corrupt; translated as noxium ('harmful'), which is uncertain. The final clause 'mundum, quem eruderastis concessae a deo' is awkward; 'concessae' is taken with the addressees ('granted by God'). In XIII: 'UOB facere' is obscure, perhaps nos facere; 'fastus' read as fastos ('annals'); 'nonus' read as nouus; 'fortis optinere' perhaps fortius (facias) optinere; the rendering is tentative. In the title of XII, 'ad laudem provectus' probably refers to Arator's advancement to delivering laudatory declamations, which is uncertain.

14.1: 'ei uestro nunc' read as 'in uestro nunc'; 'dum prouocetis parcitis' is corrupt (the verb anticipates the following 'prouocetis'), rendered as 'while you spare [the guilty]'; 'studio falsitatis: usu honestatis' is awkwardly punctuated and the sense is uncertain. 15.1: 'reduciter' read as 'reducitur'; 'submitters' as 'submittere'. 16.1: 'indices' read as 'iudices', 'inuerunt' as 'iuuerunt', 'exhausts' as 'exhausta'; 'quem potius habuimus' read as 'quid'; 'comitate' read as 'comitante'; 'certas' taken as 'you strive'.

17.1: 'denegaui' read as 'denegauit'; 'id genii' read as 'id ingenii'; 'districts' read as 'districta'. The clause 'quod reparatus in prosapie annis uiridioribus non merebat' is obscure, and 'prosapie' may be corrupt; the rendering is tentative. 18.1: 'PABRICIDAE' read as 'parricidae'; 'parricide' as 'parricida'; 'ant' as 'aut'; 'extinctos' as 'extinctus'; 'areis' read as 'arcis' (the holder of the citadel, i.e. the tyrant); the final 'P' taken as a misread question mark. The sentence 'quantis successibus ... peruenienti' is garbled, and the first 'peruenienti' is taken as 'peruenisti'. The punctuation around 'abiuratorem dulcedinis. inmoderata nuntiaret erectio' has been joined into one sentence. 19.1: 'nonum' read as 'nouum'; the opening clause ('deductus ... census') is taken as an ablative absolute ('deducto censu').

Several evident scanning errors read as intended: 'at' as 'et', 'qu honor' as 'quis honor', 'procurante be' as 'procurante te', 'superoram' as 'superorum', 'luee' as 'luce', 'KON' as 'NON', 'ant ... ant' as 'aut ... aut', 'redemption' as 'redemptione', 'tueter' as 'tuetur', 'coamento' as 'coagmento'. In XX, 'Dione' stands for Venus. In XX the sentence 'si te ... laesisset?' is obscure and is rendered tentatively. In XXI, 'demerent' is taken as 'demererent' ('can earn'). The sense of 'quo omine' and of 'inprobati more ... examinis' is uncertain.

Several scanning errors read as evident: euadeilto = euadente; pope. scisse = poposcisse; innotesctit = innotescit; ostentum eat = ostentum est; i* iactatio = iactatio; loeuta eat = locuta est; nou = non; ei pendite probably perpendite; contritem = contritum. 'si ualet iactatio' and 'proficit uentoso munimini…' are obscure; rendered literally. 'excusantem' (ab8 section) uncertain in construction. 'inuidiam iuuentutis' rendered as the resentment directed at youth; sense uncertain.

22.3: 'quos tuetur inter, inter' is taken as a dittography; 'retidiuam' read as 'rediuiuam', 'defrudater' as 'defraudetur', 'indicunteorum' as 'indicunt eorum'. The text marks a lacuna after 'dici credo aliud'. In this pagan declamation 'pontifex' and 'antistes' are rendered 'priest' rather than the glossary's 'bishop'. 23.1: 'indices' read as 'iudices', 'psrseuelorantiae' as 'perseuerantiae', 'me quod' as 'ne quod'; the sentence 'nec odiosus parcere potuit nec quem mentiris amasse percutere' is obscure and the rendering is tentative. 24.6: 'comite' is perhaps for 'comitamini' or 'comitate'; the sense 'attend' is assumed. 24.7: the clause 'nec, dura castimoniae obscenitatis euisceratione mollire' seems corrupt and is translated as far as it can be read; 'poterat forma. nesciri' is taken as 'poterat ... nesciri'; the final 'nec aneant uota recipere' is probably corrupt (perhaps 'ament'), so the rendering is tentative.

25: 'paremus' read as 'parimus' (we bear). 'uideo quod irae proficit perire conpendio' is obscure; rendering tentative. 'Achillis mei minui commodis...' taken as alluding to Hector's body ransomed for its weight. 26: the second clause ('debito tempos rogo ... eam ... consenuit') seems corrupt; translated for the evident sense (the culprit consumed on a pyre with his whole people). 'doloris meum' read as 'dolorem meum'. 'et placari n.' is broken off and left as [...]. 'ei non' read as 'an non' (a question). 27: 'cum suis cautibus' (literally 'with his crags') is doubtful; rendered as 'with his caution'. The second sentence is ambiguous as to whether Antaeus or Hercules is the subject. 28.1 quotes Virgil, Aeneid 4.365. In 28.3 the opening '4 Verg. Aen. im 866' is footnote apparatus from the printed page (a reference to Aeneid 4.365–366), and it has been omitted. 'uocates' is read as 'uocatus' and 'm furore' as 'in furore'. In 'perire innocens ante cupio quam merentem', the sense 'than [see] him perish deserving it' is tentative. 28.4 contains four hexameters printed as a single line.

nodes.text: SPEECHES.
I. SPEECH ON THE ANNIVERSARY OF LAURENTIUS, BISHOP OF MILAN.

How long will sluggish diffidence let me hide within a narrow inner chamber? How long will excessive caution, passing the bounds of honourable fear, incur the very loss of reputation it avoids? For in the experience of things it happens among men that, just as much of one's good name is plucked away by boldness, no less of it is lost through superfluous fear. For a man should not be marked as one who grabs at greedy praise, nor be charged with a desire to show off an affected devotion, when he carries out a task that lays him open to shame because he is driven by the spurs of love. For just as the craving for glory, when it is sought through speech, drives a man into shadow, so failing to render what you know is owed declares that night is near. To write superfluous things is a matter of vainglory; to keep silent about necessary things is contempt. Often the concealed praise of a teacher is the mother of reproach against us. Someone, perhaps, may say, intending to advise, that the meagre leanness of an exhausted talent, crushed by the greatness of the task, dries up, and that chatter, deprived of the strength to speak, buys failure from abundance: as if, should you pour a drop of trickling eloquence into the bed of a great river, you would in no way advance its course by the outlay of the liquid, and what is fitted to the waves scarcely brings forth any moisture. But we judge in our mind that what is said is measured by the merit of the subject of the speech; and a vein that is parched by nature often flows because of its theme: the thinness of eloquence grows rich from its subject. Often the things to be said are supplied by the merits of those to whom a speech has bound itself, especially if the speaker serves in praising out of pure affection: then affection pours forth an abundance of words; then love suggests what talent denies. Being about to speak, so far as my mediocrity allows, of the good qualities of holy Laurentius, I undertake a work full of labour indeed, but full of love. Let fear, then, be gone, the enemy of a reverent purpose: a mind subject to terror is a fugitive from glory, as the apostle Paul cries out: perfect love casts out fear; that is to say, and to show by a sure sign, that he who is afraid does not love. He is overcome without blame by the vastness of the burden who, though unequal to it, yet comes forward devotedly to carry the load. Since this is so, why should I not celebrate the feast of the newborn year with a speech of good wishes? Why should I dishonour the beginning of a bright anniversary with the ugliness of silence? Joy without speech is withered; and to hide what you rejoice in is a semblance of grief, and to have no voice in gladness is an imitation of affliction. Shall I then, holy father, conscious of my duty, not offer you words? It pleases me, however, to draw the opening of my speech from the season of your consecration, and with the flowery infancy of the reborn year to grow green in my speech, if I can: now, when the earth's sap runs through the veins of dry shrubs into buds, and the belly of the dry tinder swells, wedded with moisture; when the leafy tresses of the young shoots unfold into the caressing light, and all the weaving of the branches spreads out, or the adornments of the leaves, which nature had bound tight within their sheath, are loosed; when the song of birds is graced with modulated sweetness; when the life of the crops, buried in the clods of winter, is conceived as though released from the bars of cold and warmed by mildness; now, when the farmer measures his hope of fruit in white blossom; when the sunny beauty of the vineyards is woven by the mutual arms of the vine-shoots, and cultivation composes a fruitful face before the time of ripeness, giving grace with the taming pruning-hook and restraining barren luxuriance with fruit-bearing iron; when the rage of the deep sea passes into a gentle whisper, and the ferocity of the winds, enervated by warmth, turns into the delight of the sailor; when it is safe to launch the skiff upon the sea and to loosen the bite of the anchors, while the breaking of the storms, which until now terrified sailors, invites [them], and over the wet expanses of the sea allows the helmsman sleep; when the meadows, marked with jewelled colour, grow rich with the wealth of spring, and the elements bear witness to nature's joy at the ordination of the highest bishop. Shall I not then render to you now, bishop, what I have already learned to offer to others, you whom gravity, modesty, chastity and grace brought to the pontifical summit, who, with so many endowments gathered as if into a heap, took up the hoary dignity of your present office, possessing the ornaments of virtues so great that any single one of them would make a proven priest? I pass over the harmony of all in your election, and I do not recount the concordant judgment of different nations: let him put such things in place of praise who lacks anything he could proclaim about character. For the popular breeze is often driven by the impulses of uncertain favour, and the crowd of Quirites, knowing nothing of examination, loves the unknown while it is carried away by partisanship. In your case, he held the scales who showed himself either the partner or the author of your candidacy. The gathering of the unskilled multitude weighed your merit on the balance of a perfect man, and while the variety of your ornaments pleased, as though you had been appointed sole heir of the most diverse [qualities], so each person judged that what he approved in your distinction was enough, because all your good qualities could by no means be known to all, and you had drawn everyone individually to the favour of your star: by showing one that you are pious, another that you are stern, another that you are a distributor of a well-acquired patrimony, another that you know how to keep what was rightly gained. The whole community took up this zeal, so that, while each prevailed concerning the praise he had put forward, yet in comparison he was outdone by another in your commendations with a better title.

I do not wish to dwell on these things longer. I must come to the exercises of your labour, since I, who am not fit for the greatest things in praising you, do not know how to be content with small ones. While you were still unsteady in the new footsteps of the dignity laid upon you, the adversity of an inescapable time received you, and wars waged against liberty made the recruit of the episcopate a most practised soldier. You did not know how to fear the savagery of the robber; you, with the shield of constancy, spat out the poisons of flatteries, which among the malicious is the more harmful weapon. How often did he who could not [overcome you] by combat assail you with treacherous honours? How often did he believe that you would take up the fictions of his service at the cost of your good reputation, demanding this of you: that you should bring in the enemy by collusion and shut him within the city walls, and hand over the limbs of your sheep to be torn apart by wolves, [committing] a crime that is wicked to speak of, while he suggested the examples of many? These things you scorned as things to be shunned, and, keeping them for the vengeance of a calmer time, you committed them to memory, retaining the detestable things lest they pass unpunished through forgetfulness, and owing greater horror to the excesses, while you feared the ruin of others. But, setting aside the obstacles to speaking, let us come to those things which are more worthy of religious remembrance. When the hostile invasion was dragging the Christian people off in different directions like cattle, you were taken captive in all of them by various kinds of tortures; you, stricken with fatherly compassion, endured the torments of many, as the apostle says: which of you is tormented, and I am not? Yet amid these things adversity did not see you broken: the enemy felt this plucked from his triumphs, that he did not subdue the spirit of the captive bishop. You still fought for the release of very many, and, fearing nothing for yourself, you revealed [your concern] from the anxiety of your people. I do not wish to dwell longer on sad things; I do not wish to unfold the tragedy of that evil time; sampling a few things from your illustrious way of life, I fly past them, lest in telling of you I compel you to endure again what you suffered: although the teacher of the Gentiles recalls that he was exercised in tribulation, crying out: when I am weak, then I am strong. I pass over hunger, cold, injuries, and those increases of sickness which the enemy's mind provided for you. But, I suppose, these were childish things, and limbs strong with the sap of former health endured them. Was it not so that, when your limbs were enfeebled at the joints and long since drawn away from their own capacity by great age, your soul alone, not knowing how to be bent, endured, and, made firm by the wall of constancy, fought against its assailants with a resolve worthy of imitation? After these things Christ our Redeemer, never despising pious prayers, came to [restore] the reviving condition of longed-for liberty, and with skilful remedy makes firm the broken strength of the Roman name: a crushed state returned to health-giving vigour. When the heavenly Lord looked down from on high with kindly eyes, the light of its own bishop was restored to the city of the Milanese. Then, when inhabitants were few, when there was wandering in the houses and confused running through the sweet thresholds of the bedchambers, when there was fear and mourning everywhere and the temples of God, assigned as dwellings for wild beasts, lay filthy, when withered neglect had clouded the once most splendid halls with the mould of long-standing damp: you gave joy to others by your return; you returned to tears. Then, as with birds, when the earth is clothed with snow and in the hope of food is stripped bare by the scarcity of some place, you could see the remnants of the people that had been able to remain flock together, and the herds run from everywhere into the presence of the good shepherd, the woods wearied with their bleating. Some you then soothed with your address by a manifold kind of support, others you restored by your outlay, others you encouraged by your example. Shortly afterwards the city, already buried, recovered its former condition, which it owes to you after God, and the city which did not believe that what it had been could be restored in itself began now to strive for better things. Then, as is the way of life, one could see all things being drawn on to wider progress by good successes.

I run through each matter, briefly relating things that need a long narrative, so as to arrive at the contest of your life, at the celebrity of your highest purpose. After a time of uncertainty, a second captivity arose in the Roman church, which drew you, as though you had long been idle and a shirker of labour, from the bosom of long quiet, when the arms of your labour, scarcely laid down in the hope of peace, were taken up again. Silence would indeed be owed in a matter to be mourned, if the judgment of your praise did not drag me on, so that the abominable affair might perish from memory within a single generation. There the senate of the heavenly court was summoned; there a crowd of bishops flocked together from various provinces, where that assembly brought as many varieties of opinion as there were kinds of men; but those in whom there was the spiritual savour of understanding held you, out of love, as the leader of the chief deliberation. How then you tamed the onset of threats with the honey of flatteries, how you broke the hearts of the proud by the uplifting of reverend humility, how you grounded the minds of the wavering with the root of counsel, I cannot explain. Whoever is eager to know the history of the affair I direct to the contemplation of the deed. So many chosen men followed you alone, and the leading men of so many great cities came round to your opinion. He who formerly broke away in raw obstinacy is now seared by the heat of lamentation, and he who was separated has nothing for consolation except the tears of calamity. Perhaps some malicious interpreter of events may say: what decision has the present case obtained from such constancy? Let him ask what outcome came of the praised toil. To him I will confidently reply: that through you as bishop it was brought about that the fury of others did not receive priests as its servants, and that the sentence of bishops did not serve the indignation of those rushing headlong, lest those wrongly stirred should draw into practice [the belief] that what they wished could come about. Finally, let the talkativeness of the wicked fall silent, at least by consideration of this secret: that the fires of hatred, which blazed not from the guilt of the one attacked but from the kindling of partisanship, could not be quenched even by the fountain of holy deliberation. To you, then, is owed the guarding of the venerable canons; to you, that whatever wickedness rages at present has happened without stain on the episcopate; to you was laid open what accusers concealed from others with secret fraud; by you it was discovered that hatred must not be satisfied whenever the one who attacks is deserted by good faith. But these things are better kept for other times of narration. Hail, star of the churches, and, as an imitator of Abraham, go on to a good old age, since it is a testimony of uprightness that a man is preserved long in the citadel of the church, as it is written: men of blood and deceit shall not live out half their days. Ripe in age, and youthful for religious toil, may you prevail; set examples before good disciples with praiseworthy piety; correct the wicked with severity; and, fastened by the clasp of both good works, endure without stain in testimony of the highest glory.
II. A speech sent to Honoratus, bishop of Novara, for the dedication of the basilica of the Apostles, where there had been a temple of idols.

I believe, dearest brothers, that you revere with all the care of your mind the fact that in this place, while the name of temple remains, the old worship has perished in favour of religion; that the reverence of a shrine is established now that the libations have been driven out; that it is rightly called a sanctuary, since it has forsworn its former victims and, in the change of the sacrifice that is burnt, has taken the name of a divine house; and finally that the foundations have passed into another state with the roof unshaken, and, though human toil has added little to the structure, whatever existed has been renewed while it remains as a whole. How great a miracle must this be reckoned, where the building, though it keeps its measure, does not yet cease to rise, and, set on its ancient footprints, is lifted up by increase? We must surely ask who was the author of this work and of this renewal: none other than my insignificance's predecessor, the venerable bishop Victor, on whom divinity bestowed a name that foretold his future innocence. For with one who came to the contests undertaken against worldly vices with their outcome already foretold, once you have learned the name you know the deeds. He, through spiritual combat, as befitted a victor, triumphed over sins, and whatever the sinister portion heaps upon mortals, you need not ask about his fall in it, since you understand that he was named for what he was called. His merits would demand a wide field of oration, if either the meagreness of my talent or of my merit allowed me to advance further; for it is a certain nobility of conduct to be found worthy of the praise of great men. While our mediocrity follows him in the care of building, it has brought his vows to completion under God's auspices. Let no one think what I have said arrogant: it is right to join one's vows with one whom one cannot equal in action, since it is an assertion of conscience to follow the better man in any respect. He never, as we judge, falls into a dark path who follows the one he knows to hold out the light of life. Yet let us set out more clearly, by the office of speech, the truth of what was done. Here of old men worshipped images dedicated to deceitful illusions and drenched in the foul gore of cattle; here, to the injury of divinity, on an altar heaped with ill-omened offerings, they presented to demons things owed to heaven; here the entrails of heifers, quivering with half-alive movements, sang the future to the wretched inquirer; from here smoke, spread with filthy contagions over much, polluted the very air. In the end, from here the multitude of victims slaughtered by butchers put to flight whatever is God, while spelt, blood, incense and wether-lambs were offered to idols; while an age hostile to Christ did not accept the simple rite and, with its wealth labouring under manifold offerings, purchased the offence of heaven. I should like to go through each detail and unlock with the key of the tongue the secrets of deadly deeds, did we not rightly judge it an injury to the mouth to narrate filthy things, and that what struck them down in the doing should defile us in the speaking. Let us meanwhile set out by what successes these things have been changed, and by how great a splendour the night has been overtaken and fled. Where are the images of the gods, fashioned by the vows of those who made them, whose faces hung on the power of the craftsman, to which either the worker's diligence or the metal gave their value? Where are the gods to whom men gave power by the gleam of gems? Behold, I see, all these have fled as soon as, I believe, Christ entered: let us consider by whose aid he is supported. With him came the rays of the heavens, the diadems of the apostles, Peter and Paul. For who would be needed in the restoration of a house but an architect and a rock? but a stone and one who builds upon it? but a foundation and a workman? Why do you, dangers of mortals, tremble? Why do you prepare flight in anxious haste? He is the one from whom no slip hides your cunning, who, though he does not move from his place, follows wherever you go. Come then, most holy Lord, and glide in fully to the consecration of your work; come, and through the baptism of the human heart let these temples, until now dedicated to a foul patronage, be cleansed. Establish, Lord, sacrifices by changing them, and while we heap the holy altars with pure gifts, set among them the presence of your majesty, summoned by the merit of holy bishops, and especially by the conscience of our father Laurentius here present, who, full of so many gifts, has raised up the heights of the Church, each one of which would have made a supreme bishop; in whom flourish modesty, the chief of good work and mother of honour, patience, the nurse of holy religion, and piety that will always appease God; who has given instruction in life to the members of the Church not by speech but by examples; who, as he walks ahead, shows every path by which one goes to God, with the help of our Lord Jesus Christ, who reigns with the Father for ever and ever. Amen.
III. A speech given to Stephanus, vir spectabilis, the vicarius, to be delivered to bishop Maximus.

A mind devoted to the praises of bishops reveals the vow of a religious conscience: it is a proof of talent to dedicate what we say to those obedient to God. In their commendations a narrow speech may perhaps publish unskilfulness, yet, if it holds back, it reveals speechlessness. Who would think that narration beggarly which vows enrich? Often among the gifts of eloquence the speaker's vein is found poor, and on the other hand the treasure of the heart shines out in poverty of words. He who judges in God's stead does not desire painted conversation, but that which the unpainted brightness of the mind commends, since in the one eloquence flatters even without love, while in the other naked truth commends its own splendour. Everything that affection dictates is without trappings; those things are fashioned to a nicety which we wish to have not so much the appearance of right as a likeness of it. My speech is to you, my venerable bishop Maximus, in whom, as a testimony of merits, virtue began from your name, in whom conduct declares what the name proclaims: the provident care of your parents wished you to be chosen before you were proved. Long ago, when you were attached to secular titles, the toil of the camp trained you, and the adverse side strengthened you for the helm of the Church, as God speaks through the prophet: he who is faithful in a little is faithful also in much. The judge of sacred things earned you as companion both in counsel and in labour. Rightly were you to be initiated at the venerable altars, since even in lay life you chose what was sacred. You were found a guardian of chastity at that age in which even the law yields to desires; for it is enough to shudder at the ambition of boyhood, which licence props up. Christ seeks among hostile battle-lines his soldiers whom he will raise to the role of commander. Admitted to the Church, you fulfilled the bishop in your deeds before the time of the dignity. Your kindness was no newcomer: resting on the roots of nature, it showed its shoot from a white blossom. Everything feigned is temporary; what ripens with age is lasting. We believe the priesthood came to you not as a gift but as a reward. Others the breeze of the crowd commends, with favour pandering; to you strict rigour toward the guilty has given affection. Singular wisdom abides in you, which, though it is to be desired generally, is yet necessary in a teacher. In vain does he take on the role of admonisher who cannot weigh the burden of the office laid on him: he who is higher in honour must be compared to the basest unless he excels in knowledge. The matter of judgement, not of favour, gave you your summit: worthy of a bishop is the love that discernment wins; he who wishes to please by favour alone mars the genius of a teacher. You, taught and formed by these benefits of heaven, instruct the people more by doing than by speaking. Those admonitions which are offered by example clear away the occasion of disciples' sins: shamelessly does he invite to innocence who has not himself pursued it. Those who plan to sin fear you, as a witness, even in the secret of inner rooms: fear and reverence of you deny effect to faults as they are born. He who meets vices at their beginnings both removes the occasion of falling and purges the author of desire. These things I have dedicated to your blessedness, as if briefly, for the commendation of my tongue. If success in life smiles on your prayers, I shall consecrate myself to a full account of your deeds, so that what is known to all may be preserved in letters that will last into posterity, so that the age to follow may rejoice.
IIII. A speech sent to bishop Maximus for a dedication.

Let a poor vein of talent never be feared where the reason for speaking is rich. Our mind passes beyond the human whenever it serves heavenly worship, nor is the thinness of narration reduced to straits if the narrator renders obedience to his Maker. For he who bestowed it can adorn the tongue with the gifts of eloquence, and give genius to words, he whom we confess to have given speech. For he once helped the meagreness of prophetic utterance, when the feeble speechlessness of Moses was raised to the perfect eloquence of a master and to the trumpet of a most mighty admonisher; who flowered by no degrees while he practised his skill, nor climbed to the harvest of perfection through the knowledge of any age, who, while he bore the soldier with an unwrought talent, when ordered to seize the office of commander, because he modestly refused, steadfastly fulfilled it. So we, celebrating the feast of dedication, await grace among the blessings of spiritual joy, while we obey. Away with weak fear; let confidence conceived vainly through study be removed. We neither presume nor fear anything from the pattern of human perfection. Then who, in <praise> of blessed John, prophet and apostle, whose entry has sanctified this temple, would hesitate to open even a mute mouth? Since in him grace was older than nature, when he had fulfilled the office of a holy prophet before his entry into the light, he marked the threshold of this life by power. For at one and the same time he made his mother noble by fruitfulness and moved his father's unserviceable lips to their former speech, as use returned. Let no one naming John, after the miracles of the preceding example, suspect that he will keep his former unskilfulness of tongue. After most holy Zacharias, to whose throat humanity, once banished, returned through this name, John the apostle is rightly believed by all to be the key of words. In his company, Antoninus, hero of an ancient age, and the joined brightness of most blessed Cassianus make of the building a sacrament, of an earthly dwelling a heavenly college, of things made by hand something that no old age can violate. For things offered to God do not know decline, nor, propped up by piety, are they sent to trembling decay: the solidity of the structure that Christ enters stands firm, and, forgetting its original frailty, it gains strength from its possessor. Mean roofs are adorned by the nobility of the one consecrating them, while a perishable thing is granted to have its value from its lord. But you, most holy brother, offerer of this building, rejoice in the repayment of your reward. Hope does not know how to waver when the fruit of good action is promised to it: confidence in recompense descends from practice, and he who meditates praiseworthy things wavers in no uncertainty.
V. A speech of a bishop at the start [of his office].

A teacher who is just beginning is indeed the equal of his disciples, and in his first days a teacher is in no way of higher standing than his hearers: honour is owed to tested talents; those not yet proved scarcely claim middling [esteem]. Those are true praises which long sweat has drawn out: whenever glory heaped on [a man] comes before labour, it is flattery, not judgement. Let a soldier count among his stains whatever triumphs he gains before the trial of the field. Those who enter the Olympic contests with hurried steps, do they have any hope of a crown before the contest is finished, when the apostle says: 'No one is crowned unless he has contended lawfully'? See, praise before merit does not befit even those from whom it is rightly demanded after labour. Our condition, by contrast, stands a long road away, since as much is plucked from the fruit of our innocence as is added from our labour. For, as we judge while placed in our apprenticeship, the road is full of necessity and danger, on which a praiseworthy life must be pursued, and that life becomes most rich in reproaches if it longs to be praised by men. If our conduct is puffed up by its own good deeds, it will grow foul, as the divine words declare: 'Those who praise you lead you astray, and overturn the paths of your feet.' Let deeds, not the tongue, bear witness to a bishop's splendour: the brightness of this office shines more by the proof of truth than of speech. See, you perceive how safe is the case of the one who is subject, and to how many dangers that of the one set over [others] is joined. You will be able to support my duties more with groans than with shouting. Let no one think excellent what panders to the ears: our speech, unless it heals the soul, is worthless. Prefer him who with a spiritual sickle clears the inner parts of thorns. Then is the diadem precious, when the church's flock does not resist his persuasion as it walks toward uprightness. He loves his admonisher without pretence and with a mouth at rest who follows his teachings. Add that our inexperience bears a just fear from its very newness, since we, lately brought from the sheepfolds to guarding, are growing used to becoming, by the necessity of all, an object of suspicion, and he for whom caution on his own behalf was scarcely reliable takes up the office of one who must fear for everything. We know how much humbler toward those who serve he must be who is called to a religious command. It is necessary that he whose task it is to command thus should obey even persons of the lowest condition. For the teacher of the Gentiles says: 'I have become all things to all, that I might gain all.' Only let the working of the Godhead be present at its own gift, and make worthy him whom it did not find worthy of so great a summit.
PRAYER OF THE MASSES.

It is fitting and right. Truly it is fitting that at the beginnings of [this] dignity we should make supplication to you, the Lord of beginnings, who strengthened the infancy of the world itself, as it came forth into new light, with a power as great as the secret of your goodness with which you began it. The tender beginning of the world stood in wonder at itself and almost tottered, shaken by amazement at its own beauty, having received from its author only substance before knowledge of order, asking by what governance the light given to it was to turn, what end time would set to the day, whether it would always be reborn through constant settings, whether night, about to surround the world with dark embraces, would not hold it perpetually as its original possession. In this uncertainty, so that things long confused might serve fixed times, the will of our God became law; every dispensation, fixed within appointed limits, could do as much as he who created granted. So, loving maker, at the auspices of [my] priestly title, shine on us with the sun of [right] conduct: let the day of [this] office shine through clear sky from our merits; let what we are called perish by no stealth, by no blandishments of the devil; let it not be permitted to commit what is unfitting; at your command let zeal for the right pass into nature; let equal action attend our duties; with service well ordered let a blessed command grow, and let him who is foremost in dignity not be subject to [bad] morals. Through our Lord Jesus Christ.
PRAYER BEFORE MASS.

God, bestower of good things, for whom the accomplishment lies in the wish, who from the midst of the people dedicated Moses in the person of a prophet. For while he complained of weakness, by your authority he grew strong: he took up the merit of a priest while, with you as witness and judge, he cried out that he deserved nothing, he whose humility won him a summit lofty in deeds. Give grace equal to our beginnings, since we declare that a heavier offence is owed to our deeds. What we ask is not unheard of: your kindness is bound by the testimony of example. You will be the more merciful toward us in the bestowal of good things, the more our substance has been made prone under the burden of sin. Give, good commander, strength worthy of your choice, since under a loving prince no lowliness disgraces a soldier. Through our Lord Jesus Christ.
VI. A SPEECH [ON THE HERETICS AND THE SYNOD].

What we have kept back for a reason must be released for a reason: for, that it may be clear that both the duties of our tongue and our silence have served appointed times, at faith's urging we break out into the duty of speech. For to speak needlessly is the same as not to have spoken when it was necessary, as the apostle says: 'Woe to me if I do not preach the gospel', and elsewhere: 'a time to be silent'. It befits us especially, whom the weight of service, set above the rest, urges, either to raise up those who do good or to restrain evil. And indeed to teach you is nothing other than to have applied the spur to those already running: for what you do by your own purpose, we are proud if we believe it owed to our instructions. But he who approves good endeavours enlarges them. It stands in your consciences how greatly Nestorius and Eutyches, twin portents of the devil's shaping, long corrupted the chaste discipline of the Eastern churches with the fornication of faithlessness, who, according to the apostle's statement, 'did not receive the love of the truth, that they might be saved, and therefore God sent them the working of error, that they should believe a lie', while that field of contentions tests Christ's soldiers through the stealthily creeping occasion of scandal, as it is written: 'There must be contests, that those who are approved may be made manifest.' With whom does the venerable remembrance of the Council of Chalcedon not live, in which Dioscorus with his followers was condemned by the pen of holy severity, and the city of Constantinople joyfully received the remains, worthy of veneration, of Flavian of holy memory, whose judgement the heavenly decrees had long since confirmed? Where among the nations is Timothy unknown, who did not shudder to become more than a parricide through the slaughter of Proterius, of revered memory? For by the persecution of a sacred bishop he outdid both the kinds and the names of crimes. Peter and Cyrus and Timothy are known, who fell while they stretched out a hand to the fallen Dioscorus: these obtained from their predecessor the inheritance both of his pursuits and of his ruin. Therefore, brothers, hold the judgement of the fathers, abiding on high and cleaving to blessed Peter, since we desire the unity of a church pure and without stain. We cannot patiently bear those who belch out vain and blasphemous things against our Christ: we know that he who does not use the remedy of the knife on rotten limbs serves the spreading diseases: for unless putrefied parts are cut off, they infect. A clash with those who strive to attack the right is a peaceful one. Who would be called back by the obstacle of fear from such wars, in which he can rejoice in a life-giving death? To what powers of this world, even if they threaten, do we think we should yield, when he who governs kingdoms commands otherwise, as the apostle says: 'The sufferings of this world are not worthy to be compared with the glory to come, which will be revealed in us'? The wavering hearts of churchmen are either troubled or delighted by the things of the present life: among them Acacius, moved from his judgement by the dread command of the devil, was ashamed to have long been a champion of the truth, and, abandoning the adornments of a glorious contest, defeated his own triumph, which he had earned with holy sweat under Basiliscus: he begrudged himself his own rewards almost at the time of obtaining them, cutting down the hope of good fruits with the sickle of faithlessness. For it is graver to have trampled on good things once tasted than on things untouched: no defence remains for a man who, after the sweet taste of justice, returns to the deadly poisons of schisms. From what we have said above has arisen what is reported to have been committed lately in the church of Constantinople. Hence we suffer sorrow without the use of voice: for those who do not obey the remedies offered rightly have had no consolation at the time when they are oppressed.
VII. A SPEECH AT THE DEDICATION OF A LECTURE HALL, WHEN THE TRANSFER TO THE FORUM WAS MADE.

As the field stirs the soldier, the sea sailors, the courts the advocate, and uncertain chances the robber, so lecture halls exercise tongues. For what reason, curse it, will urge silence in a place where the prizes of words are set? Where is the palm of oratory, if here there is favour for taciturnity? The wages of sweat are well paid where the temples of victory are; servitude is well put to flight amid the halls of liberty. Let a captive mind keep its mouth bound here: he does not recognise the forum of the Roman people, nor the school of liberal learning, who still keeps silent as if in retreats. Lodging houses may perhaps be mute: here nothing is so familiar as the pomp of speaking. The applause of the customary calling urges the genius to give Fescennine wit to wedding songs; warriors are roused by trumpets; the deep note of horns lifts up those weak in courage: friendly incitements have been given to every undertaking. What shall I do, best of teachers, while you are speaking? If I keep unfashioned words within a bashful inner chamber, you would not recognise me as like your training. Sparing in thanks, I shall offend the sacred bond of friendship if I pay neither the festival of the transfer nor the gift of praise owed to you. Hail, then, nurturer of progress, torch and splendour of free birth, who, by clearing noble shoots with laborious hoes, make them known in their fruits, who in the white blossom of a young posterity show how much is being prepared for the granaries, who call us back from the lairs of wild beasts and the dwellings of owls to the forums, from which our ancestors had departed almost a long age ago. For these places are not open to the learned on whom they have not themselves bestowed knowledge, not merely to the edge of the lips. For whose trumpet of eloquence would be recognised, unless one whose boyish rudiments of speech have become known? To you, then, these benefits are owed, that the advocate about to summon a defendant will begin his speech, formidable, amid halls already proved. To you must be ascribed the unique hope of an honourable calling, that the nobility, after a short passage of time, is going to please through liberal sweat. But where does affection carry me, unaware of your strength, not weighing the sea of the narration? It is enough, amid the celebration of a friendly place and day, to have attested my good wishes. I return to you, to whom, moved by fatherly affection, I owe the voice of one admonishing. Restore yourselves to your origin by study, restore yourselves to your birth by reading: let the radiance of speech show the light of nature; multiply your parents' titles by the effect of your knowledge; adorn the glories of your ancestors with learning. The nobility of yellow metal, unless the craftsman's hand brings it to perfection, is almost dulled by its mother's darkness, and if it is not beautified by masterly polishing, the excellence that the vein has granted it profits it nothing. The teacher's insistence is indeed helped by the endowments of purer blood, but unless they are filed, those prerogatives of birth which raise themselves up do not gleam. The rustic offspring empties its mother's breasts among the furrows, and grows used to driving the flock through the pastures while it hangs at the udders; it is set beside its father's arms while he wearies the bullocks; it grasps the right hand that commits great seeds to the earth, and on the very threshold of light rehearses the sweat of its origin. What should you do, whom excellent mothers have borne to liberal studies? You must become strangers to your richer stock, unless your training shows you noble. You have a guide in eloquence and a teacher of morals: run, spurred by the goads of your lineage, and when the promised prizes have brought you to the contest, deign to remember me, since there are votes which your encourager may receive from you after the heavenly recompense. These are the things in which it was permitted to admonish you with our voice. Weigh the diligence of my heart by considering my words: let no decked-out speech, no merely alluring narration painted with dyes delight you: seek from me not the flattering but the necessary, not the dainty but the strong. Does it help one who is about to give precepts to weave pomp? He who plans to be approved no more by his meaning than by his words empties the affection of an admonisher. Let the speech of one who corrects be adorned with weight: let him who longs to be heard hold the scales in exhortation. Let the instructor in virtue shut out applause: a speech of good character commands what it urges. If I cannot set these things out by skill in speaking, I have nevertheless learned to love them by consideration of the purpose and choice of counsel. It is a certain part of uprightness to know better things, even if you cannot fulfil them. The effect of the work follows a tested intention: he who loves the adornments of learning is next to the teacher. Yet may God join himself as companion to my wish, and may I, as their instructor, pluck in fruits, as if from a hereditary possession, what I commend to the young turfs.
VIII. A PREFACE SPOKEN FOR LUPICINUS WHEN HE WAS HANDED OVER IN THE LECTURE HALL TO DEUTERIUS, V. S.

Whenever a little flower of amomum or a harvest of cassia is widowed of its root through the plundering of a playful thumb, and the noble shoot is added to the dowry of human hands, it shows the merit of its soil by its scent and bears witness to the genius of its nature at first sight. A lofty offspring does not suffer itself to be hidden: the glory of illustrious blood is not kept in concealment: the voice of a pure origin is always heard, even in retreats. But although things stand so, it belongs to human kindness not to keep silent about what you rejoice in: he takes up little of a burden who commends what he knows to be worthy of love: he does not escape the stain of savagery who does not hasten to affirm what he knows will please by its merits. Who would refuse to praise the day? Who would fear to extol the rays of the sun in any night of words? If speech pays obedience to its theme, it receives dignity from the theme itself. So do not be troubled by the leanness of your own talent, when the cheapness of the speech is raised by the value of the subject taken up: rise, my mind, weighed down by the bundle of inexperience: right hand, you are relieved of the burden laid on you. But why are we wrapped up in long preambles? The foregoing account serves the young man present, who, I promise, will go back to [the level of] his forebears, not by the announcement of augurs, but, after God, supported by hope in your accomplishment: nor do I doubt that it will come about that you can restore to the splendour of his own people this [boy], as you have conferred it on others: for he can easily revive the glories of the ancients to whom it is given to build new things. Do not think these are merely incitements of eloquence. To you alone it has been granted either to give or to restore the distinction of ancestors. There stand before your eyes not aged monuments of the boy's [family] but recent ones. Firminus and Licerius, stars of their age, address your skill with these words:

"Receive, most learned of men, the plant of both families, and as a favourable [farmer] attend to the stalk on which you may bring forth heavy ears of grain. Scrape with hoes the rich soil, which, if it is the fibre of our stock, will surely bear [crops] to answer your labours. Teach the wedded seedlings to grow in moist bark: fit the fruit of a better scion to the teeth of the young shrub: let the success of fruits come, while the plant, more exalted from his teaching, is bitten [into] with a tender mouth by you, since, unless the farmers' mattocks have written the tamed earth three and four times over, thorn and darnel will overcome the wheat harvest. The gift of Pallas and the hoary groves are enriched with abundant berries by cultivation. India nourishes the ebony it boasts of with much sweat. The rod of the Sabaean soil makes no progress when the hand is idle. Industry brought it about that the thickets of Paestum produced roses, which labour draws out of thorns like stars of the earth. The persistence of the worker is fruitful whenever the hand is applied to rich clods. Then weary arms swell with the sap of outpoured vigour, when the fields pay the countrymen their interest in full: desire for the earth's fertility arises from exercise: one must work with ploughshares, so that the dowry of autumn may overflow through the vine-shoots. No one ever earned must foaming at his lips except him who cut back the luxuriance of the vines with the curved sickle and, in various kinds of cultivation, poured out more liquid [in sweat] than he received in wine. Such is the nature of mortals: the first stages of little children are rightly compared to shrubs; once the care of parents has plucked them from the mother's root, it must be considered to which soil it should commit them according to its wishes. After deliberation we transfer our rights to teachers. Then those whom nature granted to us become yours by instruction: then the file of studies begins to claim as much for itself as origin can scarcely prevail [to give]. For it is almost not unjust that lineage should be surpassed by comparison with learning, since a father's office has indulgence for companion, the teacher's has careful concern: the parent is made by pleasures, the instructor by labours: origin grants freedom, the admonisher makes one worthy of freedom. Therefore what is praised in a man is more yours: for no one, if the witness of eloquence is lacking, will be able to proclaim what we are born [to]. The tongue which you bestow reveals the splendour of a family: the teacher's kindness becomes the herald of the race: unlearned nobility forswears a heavenly gift. So bind with tighter bonds the slips of the shoot that strays through youth: prune with iron the branches without offspring: raise up the young turf with the warmth by which you are accustomed to make all things bear fruit. Our young man has, whichever of his own people he looks at, those whom he may follow: believe us, driven by so many goads he flies through whatever sea of knowledge he enters: he will be dug with the spurs of his lineage: through so many ranks he will find nothing but what invites him to letters. Behold, our little one stands before you, to be initiated under happy auspices, and like the victim of a just man demands the devotion of a priest: he addresses fatherly devotion with his face, that by some speech it may commend his infancy placed on the threshold of life, which he asks of his parents not by speech, but his trembling shows what he desires: we are compelled to come to the aid of the little one in his need, which his fear makes plain. Promise, young man, things worthy of your beginnings: we conceive a solid hope of your accomplishment: we hand over a good talent to an excellent teacher. Revere now the first lessons of the sacred company: those whom you see showing future light with modest sparks are advancing toward [being] stars of the Latin senate-house." Let it suffice to have said these things to you: there remains for me a brief commendation. I have presented to you a kinsman as a relative, and, as a religious, one bereft of parents. What makes for my affection toward the boy you now understand. If kinship is regarded, I cannot be free from love: if devotion friendly to my calling [is regarded], those stripped of the protection of their parents become our sons. So one bond comes from lineage: by another duty binds us. Look, venerable master, at so many hands raised in supplication for him, and in the hope of the little one consider his elders, me and yourself. The learning of a pupil is a singular kind of praise in teachers. Chiron became known by the tongue of Achilles: the merit of the follower caused the reputation of him to be loved more whose eloquence by itself perhaps could not have come out into the light. Your Maro commended his teachers by as great [qualities] as those by which he himself is known: and certainly fame did not make them known through their own merits. Our Jerome, if he had not called Gregory his teacher, would be judged better than him: but the goods of the one named must be credited to him from whom they seem to have taken their origin. In sum, as I said, the reputation of a teacher strikes heaven through the accomplishment of the pupil. Before one who knows the matter I do not reproach forgetfulness, because I recall things known. The [wishes] of those who love are greedy, [even] for things known. I pray God to join his grace as companion to your studies, that you may render most learned those you have received from me to be polished, and that their learning may become your glory indeed, but my service.
VIIII. A SPEECH. A PREFACE WHEN ARATOR ENTERED THE LECTURE HALL.

It is well known to all mortals that leisure from business produces the labour of speaking, and that once the storms of cares are banished the calm of speeches glows more brightly. Talents do not lose their day unless darkened by the clouds of occupations: the radiance of maxims looks upon those free of care, and an unencumbered mind sets off the pomp of declamations. He who rashly cleaves dark straits with oars applies to the helm a breast stripped of anxiety, and weighs the steering of the tiller by that inquiry alone which befits the master of a ship. Then the hempen reins are let loose to the winds as he wishes: then seas long free are bound with the bonds of cables, and man enters to be master over the imperious heaps of the waves, to learn the uncertainties of the routes as the stars disclose them. Then, looking at the Bosphorus, the Pleiades, Cynosura, and whatever shows the way, man's path is ordered by the guidance of the sky, provided only that the mind is gnawed by no doubt from outside occupation, and that grief, the master of inertia, does not afflict the knowledge that travels abroad. But if the mind either sleeps dulled by sluggish torpor, or, roused by various goads, is drawn off along byways, it does not know how to meet its purpose wholly, since care, the gladiator-trainer of souls, tears apart the limbs of its prudence. He is always ineffective, and is shown to be cut off from the strength of his own bulk, who cannot show in the form of his treatises how great he is. Yet it is the part of a good teacher to weigh the source of a winding rivulet, which is led to him by a nail scraping the earth, to judge what its channel is when gathered into one, what it is where it rises, and to gauge the strength of a river not from what it has received but from what it could have received. Why, venerable master, sign of freedom, testimony of good blood, file of talents, maker of meanings, I have put these words first, if you ask: I, I have spoken of myself, I confess, I have described myself, whom, amid the infancy of sleeping ignorance, various occupations and sorrow, the strong mother of inexperience, have overwhelmed, to whom it is not granted to free my neck from harsh labours, so that my mouth might be adorned with the bits of studies. That my speech is rough and shines with no polishing of diction comes from the understanding and practice that I am unlearning. You, amid your wrestling-school, the inborn palm of the tongue engages: you, forgetful of me, proud Delos numbers among her citizens. You walk about as the rich owner of the Castalian stream: but I, with barely parched lips, pour out a dripping drop of a withered liquid. You, with continual sweat and no distraction interrupting, the harvest of learning enriches as its own farmer: but to me scarcely the food of beans is held out, a pauper, from the granaries of the great. You are appointed as a fortunate right hand to support a freedom about to fall: a corner of the church encloses me, who fear even the goods of the present age. Why, I ask, did it seem good to the insignia of your eloquence some time ago to direct their eyes on me, placed so far off? There were rather others whom the ornaments of your diction might compose, to whom trappings of words acquired through Latin elegances might offer a name to live on even among posterity. It befits me only to be held by silent affection, unequal to words and set apart from duties. Why would you rouse spirits which another order of life had already subjected to itself? Why would you call back a man distant through long stretches of road, with whom, as it is wrong not to have deserved praise, so it is a crime to have been praised? These things are yours, yours, do not doubt it, or theirs, if indeed any could be found who follow [you]. Yet to the young man whom the auspices of the present day have dedicated to your lecture hall, with whom I share a like lack of eloquence, I turn my words, if you grant me pardon. Though I commend his beginnings with unwrought speech, I am excused by the commands of love. We are sent under the yoke, constrained by the necessity of affection, and while we look out for dear ones, we do not see what befits us. Although a father's speech ought to have escorted him, still the one I offer is not foreign to a father. My profession too owed you, blessed one, a speech. Happy is this omen of a name among the learned: he who is to be enriched with the fruits of knowledge promises even by his name the labour needed for studies. Cleave, excellent young man, the backs of fertile lands: press in the tooth of a ploughshare still shaped on a new anvil: practise on the soil of studies whatever best befits a ploughman. If you search thoroughly the secrets of the hidden fields, you will find there Deuterius, who with the richness of tongues may repay you the shoots with multiplied seeds, and the sweat spent. Learn now already to cut back the luxuriance of words with the sickle of art, so that the young turf may thrive under the discipline of the iron. Let whatever the barren shade of the shoots has sent out be cut away: let your vines stretch their branches only toward the hope of grapes. Such you must return to your genius: such you must look toward our wishes, and when you have adorned yourself with stalks heavy with knowledge, then it will be fitting for you to be called a great Arator. Therefore let the hope of reward nourish in you the ardour for praise. Know that it is no sport of fortune if ever a lettered man has made progress among the dregs-laden flocks of the unskilled, of whom I am the first. Do not fear the oppression by which the instructed are burdened: fallen learning has more praise than the heights of the boorish. Their conscience raises up the learned, and if ever they are set against the uncertain blasts of the times, they endure evils that are to be ascribed to the ages rather than to their deserts.

Some say that my address, which I composed in a truly rustic style in commendation of Arator, merely flattered a fortunate person, for whom a necessity that feigns affection wins favour because of the power of his father: in the service of such praise the tongue, serving only the living and the present, displays a temporary servitude, and whenever it plays in someone’s praise with painted images of words, it hides the conception of the mind with all the greater effort. For sometimes the pen grants the learned a deeper hiding-place for their thoughts, if it has enticed the ears of the undeserving with sweet poultices. But let such practices be kept apart from our purpose. It befits us both to know these things and to hate them. For the prudent shun what is known more cautiously than what is unexpected. As for me, unless love has supplied the words for the praises of friends, words dictated in the inner chamber of conscience with charity as teacher, I shall stagger along the paths of discourse under the burden of the work undertaken. Therefore to my Classicus, whom my own talent has served without deceit, I have brought speeches as indicators of my mind, because friendship between equal persons is free from suspicion of flattery, and the faithful sincerity of those who love is proved whenever what you might fear does not come from power. My Classicus does not win by commands what he does not lay upon [me] as a service. Some, however, say that for one bereft of parents, auspiciously entering the schools of letters, a religious person ought rather to have supplied the words. I called him bereft of parents, for whom through nature’s happy losses the common father and bishop has become his own. He, the consolation of the afflicted, the food of the fasting, the eye of the blind, the foot of the lame, has turned so many forms of his piety, so many degrees of his mercies, to the advancement of this person. And that talent of lord Laurentius which succours the needs of the world is exercised in the service of this little child. To whom would such a calamity not be, as I may truly say, a gracious one? Whom would it not please to have lost a father, if under a profitable exchange he is granted to have found such a one? The distinctions of so great a man, which I cannot do justice to, I do not violate with profane words. He it is whose authority is sweet, or whose sweetness is stern, who fulfils the part of teacher in the church, teacher in the house, teacher at the banquet, teacher in jests, who never does what he would not wish his followers to imitate, whose conduct, polished to the fingernail, shows the heavenly road to his disciples as he walks it: for it is lesser praise to teach well, unless you have shown by deed what is to be taught. What would my speech have furnished to the youth taken up by this man, whom a favourable outcome awaits from the merits of his guardian, and perfection from the good fortune of his orphanhood? For him the prayers of his patron suffice, through which, imbued with the best teachings, he will deserve to fall short of his origins by rising above them.
X. A SPEECH. A THANKSGIVING TO A GRAMMARIAN WHEN PARTHENIUS RECITED WELL.

When we render the thanks owed for kindnesses, I believe that we forswear boastfulness by complying with what is necessary: for no swelling of arrogance is veiled by the garment of honour when words fight not for glory but for kinship. For it is one thing to speak in order to be praised, another to speak in order not to be censured. In the one case a mind greedy for fame is subject to boastfulness; in the other, with reason preserved, it rightly converts into glory whatever has resulted from the sweat of speaking. For to just and to superfluous declamations favour is shown, even if in equal language, yet with different minds: the praises of tyrants and of good princes are indeed celebrated by one and the same mouth, nor is there any difference between the eulogies of him who deserves them and of him who usurps them. Unless the weighty minds of judges weighed the reasons for speaking, this breeze of acclamation, which comes even to the unworthy, would make no distinction. The secrets of speeches undertaken are examined by hearers not with the tongue but with the heart. In sum, it is one thing to listen to a reciter pleasantly and gladly, another to approve the feeling with which you recite. But now, leaving aside the commendations of the theme, let the infancy of our mediocrity rather speak of the matter. Parthenius, once hastening to your studies, excellent teacher, I brought to you with the introduction of my little speech, at the time when he was entering the threshold of the liberal disciplines, at the time when it was uncertain whether he would express the brilliance of his lineage by his learning: for he who has no witness to his nobility is one whose blood his instruction does not reveal. Then, therefore, we accompanied the aforesaid with a speech, when it was not permitted for our words to show what kind of man he was born, because it is always a stain on good merits to have the light of blood and be shut in by the night of rusticity, to be proclaimed by the voices of pedigrees and to lie hidden under the darkening of ignorance. Gold is nothing unless it is shaped by the hand of a craftsman, and value is joined to the tawny metal by the fashioning file: when industry ceases, slight is the brightness that has come from nature. To the work of smiths the earth owes the praise it receives for what it brings forth: by the kindness of the furnace iron, which passes from the offspring of hidden veins into solid form, is tamed, and it takes captive the savage hearts of men with a taming affection. [...] would not supply to mortals unless their backs were worked [...]; it is of art that man enters the liquid element of the sea secure, and with small risk overcomes by his ingenuity the road of death. The simplicity of farmers, mistress [of the land], while it marks out the face of the earth with arms, lays out vineyards and wrings from the offspring of trees the liquor by which health is nourished. By many signs the diligence of workers is shown either to pour in what origin did not grant, or to guard the goods it did grant. And if such is the condition of all things, with how much more praise, most learned teacher, must your care be exalted, by whose right hand liberty, now on the very point of falling, is lifted up again? By whose skill either new things are established or the glories of our ancestors preserved? Truly I confess, were it not for you, whatever talent shows would soon collapse. But why do I bind myself to the greatest things, I who cannot sustain small ones, and make a general return of thanks, I who am scarcely sufficient for one person? Abundant thanks I render you before many, most correct of men, you who by your instruction have caused Parthenius to be acknowledged by me. You removed from his breast with the hoe of knowledge the thorns and the darnel: you raised a wheat harvest with which to feed his kin, with a happy outcome in him, by showing through the discord of his families one thing to follow and another to flee! O power of your talent, to be praised beyond the human! In one and the same person you showed by what art, since both descended from his blood, what he should learn and what unlearn. May God dispose our joys to a happy outcome: far be whatever adversity threatens. There is more to be praised in you because your pupil knows how to avoid [part of] his lineage than because he strives to imitate his lineage. See, Parthenius, his kinship descending to him by both paths of his family, happily acknowledges some things and happily does not acknowledge others. How I feared that the aforesaid mixture, while it disagreed by its very diversity, would cause the better, defeated, to yield to the rule of the worse, and that, given the baseness of the times, the unlearned part would more easily reign in him! But you have shown me, ornament of your age, that I have obtained more in my kinsman than I asked. You imitated heaven in the abundance of your kindness, when with manifold outlay you surpassed the wishes of the one commending him. See, now from a wintry breast and a frozen heart the little flowers of speeches bloom, and the smiling shoots of words paint the baskets that display them: see, after barbarian mutterings, words flow from his mouth that signify humanity. If therefore I do not render a return for these gifts of yours, you may consider that you have bestowed them on one who did not deserve them. For whoever has received better successes with an idle tongue shows that he does not love what prosperity has brought.
XI. A SPEECH DELIVERED WHEN THE SON OF EUSEBIUS WAS HANDED OVER TO STUDIES.

Granted that, just as novelty does, so things interrupted bring fear, and that this happens when the face shrinks from the wear of public favour, that it becomes what it was before it learned, as, when the practice of speaking dies away, old age is led back to the infancy it had struggled out of. A colt trained in Olympic contests is confident of the palm, and if it is not weakened by idleness believes victory to be in its own power: hope always promises it the crown with effective blandishments, unless the languor of sloth shakes the prize from its speed. The skilled javelin-thrower, secure of triumphs, longs for uncertain things, and he whom glory always meets in battle is overcome by long peace. Assiduity, the nurse of talent, adorns the ivy of poets with nobler clusters and a greening appearance: when practice ceases, the mouths of approved advocates fall silent. A sailor reared on ships [crosses] the liquid sea without terror; but if he turns his life to duties on land, he no longer discerns routes by the stars nor winds by omens. If a farmer, lured by city refinement, should ever despise the ploughshare, he will be dragged off course while he marks the backs of the oxen. Therefore, as persistence is found to be the mother of each of the arts in its own work, so negligence is the stepmother of learning. Such is the condition of our speech, which we bring forth after an interval of time: bearing no known figure, it does not display the pomp it ought to have purchased with age: placing all its confidence in the kindness of the hearers, it believes pardon suffices in place of favour, and pious wishes are enough in place of merit. Stand far off, feeble fear: pity for orphanhood must be introduced, a religious duty commends the speech. What should speech endowed with the splendour of skill do, where the cause pleases even without the service of an insinuating tongue, and the matter has obtained favour? It is enough that the words win affection: both have come to your hearing with favourable omens. I shall indeed say what remains, because I shall defraud my praises by as much as remains for silence in the present case. His most noble father Eusebius, equal in character as in nature, when, pressed by his last moments, he wished to overcome the lot of humanity by a plan to profit for a long time, while with the vigour of his living soul he trod down the narrow confines of the earthly prison and was pouring himself back into spiritual dwellings, as he was called by God, and nothing human remained in his mind except a spotless love for his son, except that which no oblivion effaces even among heavenly things: him he left to me to be cherished, as one well aware [of my care], as far as his [...] allow. The words of the one entrusting him were mingled with his last sighs. I shall see what he left to others; to me, under God’s witness, he left an heir. For him, as he touches the taste of life with the edge of his lips, I pray that the flavour of liberty may be poured in, so that, drawn on by the honey of the disciplines and by the combs of knowledge from waxen houses, he may himself take for himself the nectar of the flowing element. Your praise, venerable teacher, has in him something to receive, brought to its height: from the progress of such [pupils] the fullness of your merits does not refuse increase, because the elegance of the pupil is the spotless vindication of the teacher, especially of one whose splendid lineage the time demands that you adorn with the rays of knowledge, so that the glory of his origin may advance into the most serene day, when the radiance of eloquence has shone forth in him.
XII. A SPEECH GIVEN TO ARATOR WHEN HE WAS PROMOTED TO [GIVING] PRAISE [SPEECHES]. COMPOSED IN A DAY.
THEME: THE PRAISE OF LETTERS.
PREFACE.

Let splendid letters be praised from their own wealth, for foreign adornment will add nothing to their native spirit. Fleeces drunk with dye shine more when the Chinese wears them; white gems suit Persian necks. It does no good to deck out limbs with outside lustre: natural light ennobles the stars.
NARRATION.

All things that are judged worthy of public praise must be given praise as far as one's power of speech allows: to letters, radiant with the dowry of eloquence, what is owed must be paid, because, just as a free gift shows both the wealth and the spirit of the giver, so denying what one has received reveals the greed and shamelessness of the one who withholds it. Let us pour to the divinity of letters what has flowed from their own altars. For however great the stores of praise with which this subject is honoured, with whatever abundance of words it may overflow, it is fed and filled on the produce of its own estate, because, while it captivates the eyes with its own charm amid the green places it has laid out, it does indeed have delight from its own grasses, but the harvests of talent receive greater increase through their mistress. So whoever pays interest to letters grows richer, while through more secret passages, as if through great channels, the streams that were directed to them are led back, and what you have let out drop by drop you will possess no differently than if you held the right over the Ionian sea flowing back. Who would deny a deposit of skill, except one who wants to be made a beggar while he hoards it? The fruit of this thing, wonderful to say, when poured out surges up into abundance, while it makes those who brood over it go hungry. Therefore, after heavenly aid, after the help of favour from above, supply, venerable art, the praises you may use, and rejoice in the good of your invention, in what has been directed by you. Embrace in the use of praise what sprang from you: for us nothing in this matter remains that deserves punishment or reward. If by the faithful service of our mouth we offer too little in exalting your merits, this is what you gave. We are the pipes of these rivers, and we drink nothing of the stores of the liquid entrusted to us. That you may do justice to your merits through us, flow in like the Aegean sea, like the Pegasean spring. They are before your eyes, if you keep well the examples of your own ways. Safe are whatever gems from your wealth we put out to interest. See, a diadem flashing with your light ennobles my head, and with the varied gleam of precious stones grows from its native spirit while it is fittingly displayed. From you the institutions of wisdom take their root, through you they are brought forth shaped. Without you there is no savour in the breast and no freedom in speech: you are the witness of free-born blood, you the substance of modesty; through you the tongue speaks out what the heart has well dictated; you provide a road for seeking out justice, while you clear the path choked with thorns by which the things above are sought: you make a wheat crop out of darnel, you make fertile clods out of barren minds, and you carry the heavy ears to the granaries of knowledge, so that the famine of speechlessness may not prevail. By keeping the brightness of a clean family you flood an ignoble lineage with a foreign light. A thing close to God is poured in by your kindness, since through the course of the learning handed down it is brought about, with the truth of pedigrees kept safe, that the best do not degenerate and that the bad do degenerate. Through you the deeds of the innocent, which concerned the instruction of those who follow, do not perish: by your chains past events are brought back into view and the buried come to life again: you are the instruments of memory, you the cause of piety: by your ploughshares the soil of the human breast is marked out, made ready for fruitfulness: you are the founders of religion, you the enemies of crimes: under your leadership the crimes that steal in through habit are unlearned, you through whom good things are learned: either you drive men to an upright purpose or you change a crooked one.
