By your evidence exiles are adorned, and those cut off from the heights of the world you join to heaven: bad consciences you either disdain to enter, or, once you have entered the sanctuary, you consecrate them. Far be it from letters either to change what is worthy or not to change what is harmful: no armour withdraws those clad in steel from your wounds: you reach into the inmost parts even of those whom iron has covered: by your shield-bosses the weapons aimed by adversaries are repelled, and no wicker of shields is set against the darts of your skill. You raise up those set in affliction; you soothe those placed on the cross of bodily pain, so adding increase to joys that cheerfulness, even prolonged, keeps measure: if blandishments come from you, they grow sweet. It is not permitted against your command to weep even for a dead person whom you love: you suit weddings, you suit funerals: the study of this knowledge holds the most opposite things in harmony and rejoices in embracing both sides. Would that we might honour you with longer addresses, and that brevity were not owed to your laws, from which the copiousness we long for is supplied! Through the forms of letters a voice that is to go far is safely entrusted, and is made firm without loss to itself by one who rereads it. Before you humanity lived ignorant of order, and breasts belching acorns vomited out words without measure: you make a distance between men of one nature, while knowledge of you renders them like the heavenly beings, ignorance like cattle. It is plain what the forsaken lineage of mortals was like before this harvest: for with those who have an equal coming into the light with us, there is, through the distinction you make, no single condition of wisdom. Farewell, ornaments of a better age, and possess the world you have cleared of rubble, granted by God for the remedy of the times.
XIII. A SPEECH [WHEN PATERIUS AND SEVERUS WERE HANDED OVER TO STUDIES.]

If a sailor with favourable winds happily crosses the straight course of his watery journey, if a better success leads the warrior to a triumph, if through the rhetorical fields the soldier of letters is raised higher by the judge's favour: it is ours today to rejoice in equal measure. On the theme. What have I to do with the exposed and degenerate poverty of my talent? See, we grow rich from the harvest of the speech we have undertaken, by a pleasant lot, since the merit of the report enlarges the reporter and the cause commends the pleader. Where is the dread that subjected us to itself through awareness of our lack of skill? Where the trembling of the brow, made weaker by use and practice? We forget our own merit while we speak of another's brilliance. Now we learn that others too are powerful, [and] that we make [them so], since a noble fame also gives so much to its herald. I have nothing to do with doubtful things. Splendour lights up those who praise it, and the sun opens up those sunk in darkness, if they remember it. But again cheerfulness is joined with dread, and trembling becomes the companion of exultation. When does one who is unequal to small things suffice for the highest? For whoever does not commend brilliance with the light of the pen clouds it, and just as small things grow through the talent of the eloquent, so the greatest are robbed of their beauty by dryness, and unless you take up the burden after weighing your strength, you will sink beneath it. See, Paterius and Severus, ornaments of the curule chairs and names of ancestral purple, await their inherited learning at the very beginnings of life, disdaining not to drink in diligence in study together with the taste of light, whom nature gave at times not distinct to the day and to letters. For them, what ancestral glories, what ancient insignia should I, a new reporter, instil into your minds? I shall be relieved of this burden if you, hearer, consult the annals on my behalf: with me are the centuries, with me that solemn clamour of the Field, with me both the palace and the senate-house venerate Severus and Paterius: and though their family has earned the ivory staffs and the robes of state, yet, setting aside for the moment the dowry of blood, they have won by their character something that knows no setting through offices and after the tomb. I lie, unless Paterius lives in the esteem of the learned and, fashioned in lasting bronze, presents among the skilled that image made noble by the palms of eloquence. Their offspring, still small indeed, yet already very great, showing the jewelled faces of a budding little flower, implores the protection of a voice which it will one day itself provide, asking this by the plea of a silent conversation. Help the little ones whom you will soon have as fathers of the fatherland: give protection to your defenders and fight for the tender ones, so that we, more advanced in age, do not succumb while fighting for all. You know which house toils for the general calamity, to whom sacrifice is owed for the common safety, from whom has flowed the fact that amid adversity civil concord does not waver among you. Our origin owes you this tributary service, that it should always nourish without interruption guardians of its fatherland. Therefore, if the good qualities of our stock are known to you, suggest what is to be grafted in, so that cultivation may improve what shines in the seed, so that the soil, seconding the root, may have fruits; what it yields is not foreign, what we ask is not fleeting. If for the Elean and Olympic contests a colt is reared that is valued from its parents, let us be strengthened by the examples of fathers still advancing. Fortune has shown you so much indulgence, since the posterity of your champions is growing up and the protection of father and grandfather has not yet failed. Therefore, venerable teacher, receive him, spurred on by these goads and bringing the voices of all, and lend a kindly conscience to the pleas of his native soil: consider our judgements of you and, lifted up by the thought of your merit, make yourself equal to the opinion of many: labour that our defence may be made firm under your instruction and, lest the hostile assault of battering-rams prevail, join the arms of study to the walls of the fatherland. We know whose offspring is entrusted to you: see to it that industry strengthens what nature has brought forth strong. It will be the fault of the leader, not of the origin, if one born of a brave man's stock feels fear in war. It is enough for you to grow by the sweat of your instruction in such a way that you make the present boys attain the pattern of the ancients more strongly. But perhaps you will say: although a holier profession presses you, the care of these matters does not hold me last. I am the one to whom the womb of the sacred font, mother and virgin, brought forth Paterius as a son: in the second birth or re-creation of his soul I am the father. Therefore the particular provision for his education concerns me, who have been called his father even among heavenly things.
XIV. A SPEECH AGAINST AN ENVOY WHO BETRAYED HIS FATHERLAND TO THE ENEMY.

If a crime is more outrageous when a person worthy of veneration has committed it, you have, judges, in one man two things utterly opposed: the deserts of a traitor and the sacred office of an envoy. But my voice is overcome at the very outset: I scarcely believe the deed of which I accuse him. Who would suppose that consummate treachery had fallen under a title of integrity? We are compelled to say this, because a traitor fears no evil and a true envoy commits none. Why do you set your title against my accusation in place of innocence? You could escape your pursuer if in your deserts you were what you are called. No one is more cautiously wicked than he who hides under the name of loyalty: safe is the practice of iniquity that is covered with the garment of honour. Away with a purpose that rests on tricks rather than on the mind: feeble is the defence that leans on the testimony of bare honour, which will avail nothing. That you might stand against your fatherland the more harmfully, our counsels opened the way for you: it was we who brought it about that, while we sought a champion, you appeared as a stronger enemy: we would not feel the weight of hostility that you brought upon the fatherland, had it not taken its beginning from the sacred bond of friendship. We engage foreign adversaries without effort: the man who bursts out from the fruit of favour into the feeling of an enemy finds a defenceless breast: in the time of the treaty we made sure that the common adversary should not be unaware of what burdened the fatherland. For this man, most illustrious judges, if he had carried out the office he undertook carelessly, and from weariness of mind had pressed for the advantage of the allies, would deserve a capital end: what then is it to have disclosed to the enemy the inner affairs of the fatherland, for which to have fought too sluggishly was sacrilege? By what torturers must it be expiated, when you have ruined that which it is an outrage not to have helped? By what variety of pretences and deadly urbanity is he judged to have been brought to the point of being thought to fill the role of an envoy? Virtue that was not inborn is usually built up by care and nurture, and what you have done passes into disposition. By the pursuit of falsehood, through the practice of honour, he gains strength who feigns goodness over a long time. You would have kept up your captious goodwill still, had you not seen the path to harm unlocked by the key of the embassy. It is as if a physician were to come to the sick, languishing in the tossing of fevers, to bring them health, and, meaning to shut out the soul from its inmost dwelling under the guise of medicine, were to inquire: who, I ask, would not lay open to him the secrets of the vital parts and tell him in which places strength still remains? An easy opportunity of killing is furnished to the one from whom health is asked. Thus, most impure of men, by unlocking our inmost affairs we armed you against us. It now hangs on your judgement, judges, whether one who has outdone everyone in sins ought not to outdo all the guilty in punishments. Cut off the crimes that would be born hereafter: from the torment of one man will come the correction of all. It is a kind of loyalty to be severe towards an enemy of the fatherland, lest, while you spare the guilty, you provoke vices to increase.
XV. A SPEECH AGAINST A STEPMOTHER WHO, WHEN SHE COULD NOT PERSUADE HER HUSBAND TO HATE HIS STEPSON, GAVE POISON TO BOTH.

Here, judges, is the stepmother who, to satisfy her hatred, does not spare her affections; who, so that the stepson should not escape, chose to join the man she loved to his fate; who, in the manner of the most savage beasts, made a token of mingled deaths, judging worthy of the lot of death whoever could be slaughtered together with her enemy. Her bars broken, her fury found its exercise, destroying whatever came in its way as though it were marked out for death. Longing for what is ruinous to all, her anger was still growing, had the poisons not run out: the poisons she found were drunk by two: nothing remained to be kept for the death of others. Alas! how she groaned at the emptiness of the cup when she saw so few corpses, indignant with herself that she had given the dead more of the deadly liquid than was needed to kill. She sought, had it been allowed, to draw out from the entrails of the dead the price of others' deaths, so as to scatter fates among very many by drops, so that the noble venom might possess the inner chambers of souls. Before the trial the pernicious fluid was poured into the cup: it made her recognise what she had lost, after she killed few with abundant juices. Where in the world was the spirit of conjugal devotion? Where the sacred bond of marriage? The memory of the stepson weighed more than that of the marriage bed: while she obeyed her savagery, the affection for the husband before her was driven out: she believed that in anyone living the substance of the stepson could remain. The impious woman wished to confound the light and to cut down the harvest of the human race as the world collapsed, hurling headlong whatever could go to its setting, longing in her wickedness to subject our day to the ancient laws of Erebus, so that she might not, hateful as she is, look upon him even after the underworld. By how many steps and advances in crime did she descend to poison? For a long time she put off death, which at last she thrust upon him, set in torments, in place of a kindness. Before that she afflicted the hated body with lashes, hunger, cold: last in a stepmother's indignation comes the carrying out of death. I should wish, judges, to dwell longer on the accusation, were it not that a more prolix tongue would delay the criminal's punishment. We do not want her, doomed as she is, to earn a respite in the light from the time you grant to the one pleading. How often, most wicked of women, did you cherish your stepson with treacherous embraces, feigning to be a mother? How often did you contrive with harmless drinks that he should take death from your hand without suspicion? You watched for the moment of thirst and the need to drink: perhaps he begged you, so that you would offer death the sooner: you gained a reputation for kindness by obeying your stepson's wishes. How often did you take the place of mothers, so that you might show yourself a stepmother more safely? It is usual, guardians of liberty, in the partnership of marriage, for the offspring of one partner to be cared for as a common pledge, while the affection the father holds passes to the son: when wives die, husbands in their foresight, seeking partners in their cares to raise their posterity, thus find stepmothers. Yet often under this name a mother comes, the more careful towards another's offspring the more anxiously she wishes to avoid a tragic name: a mother is protected by her security and the sacredness of her name. There are some who are believed to be angry even out of compassion. Rightly do we spurn your flatteries, ill-omened women, with which you clothe your inner selves in the paint of malice. I am ashamed, most holy judges, to prolong with lengthy attack a woman condemned by her own deserts: the sentence I hold up by my labour is not in doubt. Would that she might be driven from the light by refined torments, and, cut by slow wounds, survive her own body! Let the guilty soul not be driven from its own seat at a single moment. Purity is brought back into men's hearts whenever you cleanse the eyes of all by the cross of the guilty.
XVI. A SPEECH AGAINST A MAN WHO DEMANDED MARRIAGE TO A VESTAL VIRGIN AS HIS REWARD.

Do you believe, judges, that through this man laments are mingled with victories, and that the savour of triumphs is spoiled by the reward? Do you suppose that the gods are offended at the outcome of events, and that the divine powers who helped our prayers are brought to repentance? Here is the most worthless of men, who orders us to groan because he conquered the enemies of our fatherland; who, when the battles are over, in demanding the price of his labour commends both the enemy and the wars; who thinks the votes owed to his labour exhausted unless they are bestowed with the gods angered, so that his city may lose what it is believed to have gained through him. He trusts that the spirit of a warrior is not held by painted panels and images, nor does he ask to be preserved for the ages fashioned in bronze: he thinks the only joys are those from which the gift of adultery comes. If you offered yourself to dangers for this, that what you ask for your sweat is shameful to name, we cannot owe to harlots what we have won. You did not wage war out of pious love, you who after the enemy engage with modesty in the middle of the city: in vain did you drive off the enemy, you who play their part in the triumph. We kept our state of honour free while we lay exposed to danger: the good fortune of brave men is to be shunned when through it we are joined to the miseries of the subjugated. Indeed, lights of the senate, are we to think he was brought to monstrous desires through small steps of crime? By how many degrees did practised wickedness arrive at buying vices with praises? We believed, while he lived his life in tents and drove his body by hard successes towards the marks of strength, that he was bound by love of his fellow citizens, so that through his soldiering neither fire should take the cities nor corruption the sacred virgins. For this man bought with so many wounds that no other should enjoy the fruit of crimes. What I owe you, cruellest of men, is plain to see, by whose benefits I, the victor, groan at the fate of the conquered. Tell me, guardians of liberty, what rather did we have that possessed our minds, amid the blare of trumpets, as terror, while the crop of iron and the snorting of horses threatened destruction? I believe it was that the rigid chains should not bind the free necks of the fathers, that the inviolable modesty of mothers should not perish in the city's destruction, that vowed virginity, given over to sacred rites, should not be carried off by a plunderer's fire, that chastity in service should not become the prize of an insulting enemy, that hostile violence should not steal upon bodies freed from the human condition, and that purity, brought to the last extreme, should not serve the lust of the enemy. I ask you, great-souled hero, what evil you drove from your fatherland, if as victor you desired what I feared, while the favour of the gods delivered the enemy to death by your blows. I ask whether you begged the gods above to be your helpers in that crisis? If you did, now that the dangers are past, do you threaten their priests in place of the offering you owe? If you did not bring pious prayers to the contest, what do I owe you, whom the general good fortune, accompanying you, freed without prayers of your own? If you understand, you owe the gods much if they took care of a suppliant: more, if they gave victory to one who did not ask. I suppose, on leaving the battle, you worshipped the shrines in the first place and gave thanks there, whence you strive to snatch plunder with hands that should be at rest. I fear that, though no torch consumed the temples, a fortunate lot leads away a Vestal virgin as a captive.
XVII. A SPEECH AGAINST A MAN WHO WITHHELD FOOD FROM HIS AGED FATHER. GIVEN TO ARATOR.

I do not know, judges, whether any penalty can be found that would satisfy the crimes of the accused. Meanwhile my tongue lacks resources, since the novelty of the deed outstrips its accuser. This is the son who refused his aged father food when he could have supplied it, adding this touch of ingenuity to his crimes: that he should be a parricide while his father was still alive. You think you have escaped the punishment due because you did not bring death on your father: you spared him so that you might be the guiltier. You could have ended the torments you had inflicted with your father's final end, if you had offered his throat a healing hand: the first of your evils is this contrivance, neither to ward off your own begetter's death, as befits a dutiful son, nor to inflict it, as befits a cruel one. Why is it that, between the two ways, inventor of a refined peril, you follow neither and feed on your father's drawn-out wasting? Under your management your father lived the more unhappily because under your management he did not earn death. No one, most holy [judges], doubts that the evils of this world are buried by a death that is called upon, and that the common lot is a prayer for those set in adversity: what sets a limit to bitterness must be wished for. I ask, with what beasts is he to be compared who by his management inflicts hardships without end? Whose guile, while his hand keeps off the author of his life, has produced things that would gladly be exchanged for death? Already this man's father was worn down by the burden of years: already through the old man's trembling limbs the ravages of age had overturned a once sturdy step: already, under the bites of long time, the form that declared a man was sinking into wrinkles: yet he had not reached ripe age without hope of support, for an offspring now grown smiled upon him. With greater confidence he gave away what he had gathered for his living, he who, we know, always placed his granaries in the eagerness of his child. He thought it an ill omen to take thought for property, he whose son was alive and well, thinking that this could suffice for his chill grey age, which, renewed in his offspring of greener years, he did not [need to] earn, when suddenly the splendid young man stripped his father of that security. I should like, venerable judges, to turn my words to him for a little: but I think warnings are wasted that are offered to ruined morals. Do we think, most venerable of men, that anyone's offspring comes to these duties by teaching? Nature's instruction suffices for a child, since human law pours into their breasts what teachers usually do. To fulfil what is owed is not for him a good that comes from outside, nor can those endowed with reason lack what we see to be implanted in birds. We read that eagles, in turn, are fed by the service of their young, and that the benefits of their parents, which the chicks received unfledged when they were stripped of the coverings of their eggs, they repay with a kind of strict fairness. Birds do not think they are free to refuse what they have received: what sort of nature is it that cannot imitate the winged creatures in care for one's own? I pass over the many examples of the rapacity of wolves: with fasting mouth they carry food to their parents, and the beast, its belly unfed, runs to those who begot it with its mouth full. Do you weigh the guilt of the accused, and what punishment is fitting for one who has committed unheard-of things, since vices spread through impunity, and, unless severity came to the aid of the judge, the force of sinning would go out through the whole body [of the people].
XVIII. A SPEECH AGAINST A TYRANT WHO GAVE A PARRICIDE A STATUE AMONG THE BRAVE MEN AS HIS REWARD. GIVEN TO ARATOR, VIR CLARISSIMUS.

Although, judges, the likenesses of brave men are preserved in bronze that will last for ever, and through these images they do not know death even when buried, although through these arts the image of mortals passes into eternity and human industry overcomes the narrow law of human nature: yet has a parricide ever earned the reward of valour, or has a tyrant ever paid it out, when either a criminal has drawn forth the gift meant for the innocent or an oppressor of liberty has thrust it upon him? A statue, venerable presidents, is the fruit of sweat, to be bestowed by the purest judgement, so that a fitting brightness on both sides neither disfigures the receiver, if it comes from an unworthy giver, nor, if it is conferred on the undeserving, stains the giver. If the voice of one who detests vices is free against a tyrant, if it is permitted to press charges under a guardian of crimes, I shall say what I think. An honourable thing has fluttered between two wicked men, and, protected by the defence of neither, it knew neither from whom it came nor to whom it passed. Consider into whose rights a thing long ago decreed for the brave, and to be won by the vote of their blood, has come: that a usurper of power bestows it and a slayer of his father receives it. Where I should turn I do not know: caught among the precipices of your virtues, venerable prince, I do not know whether to accuse you for being a tyrant or for honouring parricides with a reward. Both are worthy of the cross and of being driven from this present life in sacks. You do not think it enough that you have escaped the punishment owed, unless you also bestow what is not permitted and he receives what he does not deserve. Long ago you presumed these things through audacity, when as a destroyer you entered the citadel of justice, raised to dominion by the same votes by which you conferred a statue on the other. It is inevitable, most distinguished of men, that all cherish what they themselves have been, and excesses are not usefully corrected except by those who have reformed. He is lavish of his brow who believes that a follower of crimes will punish evil. A judge's conscience is bound by the constraint of its secret, and does not think itself free to condemn in its subjects what it did not hesitate to commit itself. By what successes, or by what varied advances, did you come to this, you cesspool of crimes, that on reaching the heights you were allowed to sin so far, when you wished, as to invite the disgraceful to higher things with statues? You have exchanged the taste of liberty for the gall of slavery: he turned the obedience owed to his father into swords. Consider how praiseworthy are the things you have injured, and, with the accuser's mouth at rest, judge what a father and freeborn status deserve. You bind free necks with the yoke of the most wretched condition; with him the law of nature availed nothing: you do to the fatherland what he did to his parent: in this perhaps you should be thought the crueller, that you dispense harsh commands under a kind of living death, and do not grant an end, as with a healing hand, to those to whom death is desirable: he, not suffering his father to remain in the world, snatched life from the author of his light with a swift blow. I do not know by what difference in crimes they are distinguished: meanwhile, if it is permitted, they should be joined in punishment. If the swelling of any haughtiness had raised you up against the citizens, the injured community would mark you as guilty, and your immoderate elevation would proclaim you a forswearer of the sweetness of private life. If he had looked on his begetter with a grim glance while his father was unharmed, he would have earned the name of parricide. See what is fitting for those who have reached the summit of offences. There is nothing that either the afflicted fatherland or the slain father could believe remains [to be done]. Let it be far from us, leading men, to aggravate the deed with arguments. The bare names of the accused suffice, to be shielded by no privilege of defence. I shall indeed add to the offence certain things that are the height of guilt, so that nothing may seem to be withdrawn from the case which you, I think, have found with keen tracking. The statue of a parricide is surrounded, walled in by the sides of the brave, and a likeness that either literary care produced or the Field of Mars cast is set below his image. Hard, believe me, do so many bear it that by no titles, by no reward, are they distinguished from the shedder of his father's blood, and, if any vigour remains to their souls, they weep for their rewards, which they won by the effort of their strength. Where is honour, where the efficacy of liberal study, where the reward of one who fights for his fatherland, if the holder of the citadel displays bronze forms, and he who brings about his father's funeral obtains [them]? Only exact torments worthy of their deserts, lest, if an unequal punishment condemns the accused, the praise due to right judgement is not owed to you. Let those be driven from life by one road whose lot in crime has proved almost equal.
XIX. A SPEECH GIVEN TO AMBROSE AGAINST A GAMBLER WHO GAVE THE FIELD IN WHICH HIS PARENTS WERE BURIED AS A GAMING STAKE.

After, judges, the gambler's shameful passion had broken loose, his fortune brought down to thinness, and the failure of his means gave over his growing eagerness to compete, not even his parents' tombs began to be spared from the base stake; the doubtful outcomes of chance began to be awaited over ashes, and the laughable turns of contests to be set out over tears. Where are those who say that souls which have finished with the light have nothing in common with the inhabitants of this world, and that those who have passed over have their own day after their separation from this age? See, the tombs which this man's ancestors had obtained have now almost grown old, and in very fact through length of time the tombs now need tombs themselves: and yet with this most shameless reveller the prizes of his wager are still believed not to have perished in them. After the long courses of their lives, the shades, owing nothing to chance, are ordered to await an outcome from the dice: after squandering the wealth which your parents had gathered by long thrift, after the many weights of silver and gold which frugality kept under measure to help an heir, you, offspring worse than childlessness, honoured the urns of your forebears by making them a stake at the gaming board. If a lesser care on the part of their descendants adorned the mausoleums of those who went before, the neglect would deserve punishment and would await a penalty from those judges who wish to correct their own sons' morals in the misdeeds of others. Instead of the festival returning by the fixed law of the seasons, instead of garlands and the gifts on which souls feed, you thought it a sin if your parents' tombs did not change owners. You would not have been permitted to sell these last homes even to ransom your child carried off by enemies. I ask what necessity there is that I see a stranger as owner over your parents' ashes: and nothing else is set before me but a game. O wretched condition of mortals, both when desires are denied and when they are granted more unhappily! How often did your begetters move God with anxious sighs, that they might not pass from the enjoyment of this light without a lawful heir, which is believed most ill-starred? How often had their mind, ignorant of the future, come near to death at the pallor of their child? Born, brought up, educated for this harvest, judges, he has arrived, with a mind empty of shame, at not allowing those who bestowed his patrimony to remain in his possession after he has lost everything. We condemn in the criminal a most shameful will: for it may perhaps happen that by the kindness of gentleness you have sent the bones of your forebears to upright owners. Reverence for the dead is common to all, and the whole of humanity demands fitting care for the sanctity of those laid away by their last lot: yet the last dues are paid more especially to our ancestors, whom veneration so sets before its eyes that we believe that what is done in carrying out the instructions of the dead is offered to the gods. We keep all that they commanded, not believing that a violation of their instructions happens with impunity. I find no new kind of crime with which to explain this novelty in words. For those for whom it was sacrilege not to obey, what is it to have sold their last dwellings for games? Believe, judges, that so many of this man's ancestors stand before your eyes, awaiting the time of vengeance, by whose appeasement care for parents can be sanctioned for the future, to remain without stain.
XX. A SPEECH AGAINST A MAN WHO PLACED A STATUE OF MINERVA IN A BROTHEL.

We believe that the verdict of venerable judges has always been doubtful where an offence is confused. The judge's deliberation over which way it should chiefly incline has stalled where the nature of the crime has proved doubtful: for just as manifest vices demand a judgement fitting to equity, so obscure ones hold it in suspense. When the crime is in plain light, what hope remains for the one being condemned? Grasp in your minds, I beg, and weigh in your inner judgement what kind of man this is who has violated both the eyes of virginity and the secrets of the brothel, and who, sacrilegious on both counts, neither reveres the vices, to which he has brought a hostile witness, nor fails to ruin the modesty of chastity, which he joins to the unworthy. I demand of you, portent of the human race, what worship of religion brought your fickleness to set up an image of Minerva, while the injury inflicted by the foulness of the place shows you an enemy of purity: and the corruption you have made public cries out that you show no reverence to the defilement of Venus either. Those who are drawn on to the transgression of crime by a love of excess know no limits to sinning: those who have contrived lofty crimes know no measure in their errors. While, mocking, you join together by art into one fabrication Dione and Pallas, deities most different, bound over to foreign opinions, you have made your offence the more bitter by your religion. It is a thing deserving the utmost expiation, to mix discordant things and gather into one those which you have insulted unless you keep them apart. Do you believe a man can be found who holds to neither of the world's two ways of life, and is neither a friend to the virtues nor found faithful to the vices? The patronage of faults commonly stirs some to despise good works, and those who are strangers to the taste of praise commonly rejoice in the fruit of licence. But which of these things will find you a follower? You have raised hostile hands against the better order, and yet you do not bow your neck in sincere obedience to the wicked. I hate, leading men, those who are lax judges of their own conduct; I condemn those who through neglect of clear actions are drawn into doubt: but more cursedly still do I detest those who, caught on both sides, show a steady conscience to neither. For those whom you see keeping faith with their sins promise, at the time of repentance, devotion to honour. If, most wicked of men, the remembrance of Minerva had stirred you when you were placed before the shrine of Venus, would the memory of your mind, loving both powers ill, have injured [them]? You would have fled the dwelling of her whose adversary you held in your mind. What honour is it to have placed her statue where the goddess of chastity could be violated by mere mention? Not knowing, most ill-starred man, how to approach the heights of accursed error by degrees, you have almost stirred up war again among the heaven-dwellers. Those eyes see always shameful things, having loathed embraces joined by a certain law of obscenity. While, by your arrangement, a captive deity is present in brothels, you alone have shown that the power of the gods serves human lust and that they are confined to those places to which they have been assigned by mortals. How discordant will be the outlay in burning sacrifices? The offering to one deity will do injury to the other. For since, through your foresight, the twin power of the gods has occupied a single couch, and modesty and lust have met in one temple, neither favour will look upon our devotion: those whom you have mixed in one dwelling we shall have offended by their proper sacrifices. What will the gifts be like which must be carried in a crowd by unchaste women and virgins? The one must be offended by merriment, and the other appeased by wantonness. Among the vervain and the incense there will be a contest over the victims, and the deities must be made angry by the very means by which they are soothed. I withhold a lengthy narration from sacrilege: let the accused spend among his punishments the delays he would receive in the light, since even the foulness of another's acts disfigures the one who reports it.
XXI. A SPEECH [AGAINST A CERTAIN FATHER WHO, THOUGH HE HAD NOT DEIGNED TO RANSOM HIS SON CAPTURED BY A PIRATE, YET DEMANDED TO BE SUPPORTED BY HIM].
THEME. LAW.

Let children either support their parents or be imprisoned. A certain man had two sons, one thrifty and one dissolute. Both fell among pirates. They wrote to their father about ransom. The father sold his property and went to the pirates: he was given the choice of ransoming whichever he wished, since he had brought too little ransom money. He chose to ransom the dissolute one, because he was sick. As he was returning, he died on the way. The thrifty one escaped from the pirates. The father asks him to support him. He refuses. The case taken up against Quintilian. For he defends the father, we the son. I ask you who read not to think it arrogance.
PREFACE.

Is it lawful to speak against Quintilian except for the truth? Or does eagerness to speak make him forgetful of himself who gives his words to justice? Polish suits deceivers, while eloquence, painted with the brush of falsehood, takes on a foreign beauty to be praised only as far as words go. Let equity be maintained without the comfort of the orator's art: I choose the display which defended honesty will bring forth. Let simplicity, fortified by the favour of heaven, advance against a most eloquent man: our daring springs from confidence in our side. Only grant us, leading men, your kindness, with the caution of your ears and minds kept intact, so that that loftier buskin of speech does not believe, by the power of utterance in which it excels, that victory is its own possession. What else is it to help us against his onslaught than to bring back justice, wandering abroad, after an interval?
OPENING.

I would rejoice, most distinguished judges, to have escaped the squalor of the prison and the chains of the pirates, if on my return a father had not taken the place of the pirate skiffs for me. He seeks support from me, whom he freed from the enemy neither with gold nor with tears. He thinks that the return of the one whom he did not ransom when he could ought to profit him. In vain do you implore sustenance by the benefit of the law, you who by your deeds have dissolved the rights of nature. The law decrees that food be supplied to fathers: this sacred bond does not lie merely in the name. Let even the pirate say whether you are a father. Though you often say that I was better than the dead one, you never show it when you judge. Consider the course of faults of my departed brother: he who was preferred was more like his father's character: by what omen I spent my life, driven out by these people among strangers, was made plain when my father of his own will abandoned me to the robbers. He thinks he puts forward strong arguments against his offspring when he boasts that the guilty son, near to burial, earned the greater favour. I ask, judges, pronounce what I owe. Meanwhile it is clear that I was set below even the ashes of the dissolute one. He does not blush to demand anything by a parent's authority from one to whom he refused to be what he is called. Would that the pirates' chain had kept my health for these uses! I would make my father a captive of shame by supplying undeserved support, so that the unjust arbiter would groan over the injustice of his own verdict. For food given by one whom you have deserved no good of drains you: the stomach is empty in its very fullness, which has no consciousness of a kindness rendered before. I do not know what remnant of his hope that man thinks is left from his two sons, who returned one to the earth and allowed the other to be kept under the perpetual dominion of robbers. Let him take, unless he is ashamed, whatever limbs exhausted by tortures can earn. I do not know what an old man demands of a weakened one: meanwhile, as I observe, we both need feeding. Why do you bring before us the account of your modest means? He who wished to ransom one sold his property in such a way that the price would not suffice for both. Who could set out my misfortune, who my miseries? For me, after the Cilicians, even the liberty I have regained is said to be in bondage. Tell us, we beg, judges, if even in my fatherland we are to be declared debtors, what have I escaped? My most holy begetter has added that I should grieve that the chains released my brother. As though nature demanded of us so great a servitude that the joy of a brother rescued should make up for my staying behind. We owe love to those who share our flesh once we are freed. Believe one who speaks plain things: joys over another cannot enter a man who fears for himself. For he cries out, in the manner of a disreputable test, that the one from whom something is asked is in some way the richer. Painted polish keeps such a trick in supplications, using feigned humility in place of darts, so that by the joinery of a proud self-abasement it leaves nothing free to the one who is asked. He testifies that the property was bid for both, though it is clear it was spent for one: he expects double gratitude from a single kindness. I do not know whether one should ask what he thought, when it is plain to all what he did. The pirate who granted the choice between us exhausted the defences of your side: let the father, who ransomed only the one about to die, keep the only thing he desired of his son, a tomb. For he who preferred the sick to the healthy declared that he dreaded the one who would live. What you can demand of the survivor I do not know, since you have for consolation the tears that you bought.
NARRATION.

Always, judges, even at an age friendly to sins, I kept up the cultivation of honour, withdrawing expense from boyish desires, so that maturity of years could rejoice in it. By this thrift we brought it about that something remained to my father which he could offer for his dissolute son. Why do you complain of the slenderness of the patrimony? If I had been equal in character, things would have come to such a pass that neither could have been freed. He is an unequal arbiter who chose that what we stored up by our modesty should profit the other. As far as paternal severity asserts, our honesty was the cause of our long captivity. Healthy, attentive to my father, dutiful to my brother, such a one does not deserve to be brought back to his fatherland; and had we not been captives by a single lot, our return would have been sullied by suspicion of us. We were equal in calamity, but apart in our father's love. Happy by the backing of his dissoluteness, the young man both drained beforehand a great part of the common property and was helped by what remained. Wretched me, ever a captive by my father's judgement! I rehearsed in peace beforehand what I later endured, and while I kept the path of right I learned, by the token of thrift, how one might live among enemies; hence it is that I lived content with the food that savagery provided, at the last extremity, by the comfort of habit, not by the humanity of the robber. I ask for whom that thriftier practice preserved me, if the observance of what is right earns the displeasure of fathers?
OBJECTION.

What of the fact that the barbarian declares he said, 'You have brought the price of one'? Objections always receive the reply they are owed. You were anxious about no auction: the gold you had produced you offered to the enemies' eyes before any pleas. While everything went for you in this way, no one could doubt that the freeing of one would satisfy your desires. Yet as soon as you entered those caves, filled with the squalor of death, the pirate recognized what you would choose before he granted the choice. That fearfulness did not come from love: he shows nothing doubtful who, though he had two sons, announces by every sign of care that he had come as if for one. After your departure stronger guards confined me: thanks be to the Godhead if it has protected my liberty in this too, that I escaped. Meanwhile your decision seems to have sent this word to the enemies: 'Unless the one I leave behind is carefully guarded, he will slip away.' With the gods as guides, our flight, set before the eyes of the enemy, succeeded.
DIGRESSION.

Moreover, since our father is rich in speech and has learned through length of life to make what he says seem present, skilled at imposing compulsion on minds through the ear, he says that food is common to all who live in humanity, and he demands from one what no one may refuse, alleging in general that whatever the earth has produced is owed to all. But when the cornfield poured out its wheaten offspring and the vineyards their liquor for common use, and the land was not distributed man by man to its cultivators, no one left a son among enemies in such a way that he was believed to have preferred groans to services. I do not know, judges, what he can require of the survivor after he has chosen tears. But he throws in our face the fear of the law, and he who showed nothing of a parent wants what is written between parents and children to be owed to him. He seeks our goodwill while we are compelled, and desires that we should show to filial devotion what he himself has declared that one who pleads an excuse cannot refuse to fear. Is there any place for mercy where command presses? What may not be withheld we cannot say is conferred by generosity: clemency is not so called unless it is freeborn; whatever you have not the power to refuse, if you have given it, do not count it as a sincere gift. But the frequent repetition of 'nature' and the holy name of 'begetter' will stand against us, as if the enjoyment of light, obtained by the gift of the heavenly ones, could be counted among the things bestowed by men. It is sacrilege to call the indulgence of the gods the seed of mortals: a cruel father holds testimony of his lust alone. He also adds to my burdens when he demands the comforts due to one abandoned, saying that the city could have helped him had I not returned. What else does that wish reveal, except that the pirate should take me back again? If the sight of your offspring unbought is grievous to you, surely you will at least possess without price what you are accustomed to buy dear, my tomb: my age indeed promises life, but the magnitude of the tortures, which I endured more bitterly after you left, promises death.
EXAMPLES.

Then you brought forward examples worthy of a father's purpose: but they lost their worth by your interpretation, as if hoary age had furnished your desires with a model, and not holy institutions with something to imitate. What weight did the shoulders of great Aeneas feel from the burden of his begetter? Or did he weigh down with his body the son whose bearer he himself had often been in deed? Do you want to know why he deserved to be rescued from the enemy? It is set before our eyes that he did not wish [it], lest he be a burden, believing that a burial was provided him by the ruin of falling Ilium, and, lest his aged limbs hold back his son, who was going forth and was more worthy of life, he said that the fall of the city was enough for a tomb. He wished to remain among the plunderers while his son escaped: you went back to the fatherland with your son left behind. Why do you recall the noble deeds of Scipio on behalf of his father? When he zealously offered himself for his begetter, he gave his all, but he did not use up everything he owed. The cause of good wishes is always alike, and the pursuits of kindness are not divided. He declares what he deserves of his son who reckons that the son does not come to the duties of nature unless compelled. The law threatens chains unless I obey: what does it matter? The long duration you procured has shaped me to this habit of punishments, although long endurance of penalties does not make one defiant. I wonder, however, if my father has brought upon me what I escaped from the barbarians: there is nowhere to turn away from plunderers if the same lot follows one into the fatherland: one and the same, as far as I see, is the adversity of native soil and of foreign land, and no different the bitterness for those returning and for captives. Yet I find no difference, nor do I ask which chain in particular binds my neck: whether I incur the bonds of stiff iron or pay a tax to a gullet, the condition is the same. Fasting, I will carry feasts to one who is sated and, what is worse, to one who does not love me. With what disdain will he cast away the food offered by me? With what rancour will he trample on my devotion? A man whom I could not have as merciful even when I was in extremity. He declares he knows that I and my brother equally begged for ransom by letters, implored release with equal tears, and, placed in like lot, dictated letters. I do not deny it, I do not refute it: he has the victory on this objection. But I demand this: what cause brought it about that, when two asked, what was owed to two one received? For both you entered the seas and, as you assert, crossed the threats of the liquid element with devotion as your guide. Who would believe a man returning with one about a twofold love? Mercy is never praised unless it has been put to the test: with what shame is affection proclaimed when the deed is lacking? Does the secret of the breast always become known truthfully through the key of speech? Devotion that is not held, even when mute, by deeds is a show. Love will remain with its root unshaken among all men, if boasting avails. The law says: 'Let him either support or be bound'; the father cries: 'That feeding is owed to a parent even if he does not ransom.' You have armed yourself for this role, indeed, when you ceased from the duty to which you were bound by nature: a windy defence profits by what was shamefully denied to genuine purity. Believe me, when the law spoke of the parent, it did not pass over the ransomer in silence: it urged, ordered, extorted that all the sacred obligations of a dutiful work be fully performed through these names. My calamity clouds your senses from understanding this matter: the ransom of a son, which lies in the care of kinship, could not also be among the precepts. While you praise the children of Leda, you accuse me of impiety and of envy in my brother's freeing. You do not know that, if the equality of your distribution had proceeded between them, it would have produced error: for you would have condemned one to the everlasting beauty of light, the other to the possession of perpetual night. I lie if your judgements about your sons were otherwise. What did you think it meant, when the pirate released one whom he would never have, and kept the other, whom he would never let go, as though the father were handing him over? Whatever I endured after you were out of sight in that deadly land, I do not doubt proceeded from you. All my hope was consumed after the ransomer departed from barbarian soil without me. What ships heading for those inhuman shores did I not first spy, and whatever my eyes could not follow as the sight faded, I grasped in my mind, since those who wait more eagerly see something more keenly? How often before your arrival, if ever the pirate allowed us to range the open air, did my father appear to me in strangers, and I saw those images which love paints for itself without the disgrace of lying? By these images hearts long troubled are struck. Alas! How often, when I refused the food the pirate provided, did the barbarian help me with this consolation: 'Fear nothing, sigh not at all over this affliction: if your begetter lives, you are little separated from the station of liberty.' See, at last fortune came to my desires: even the plunderer eagerly announced to me his arrival. He was not far from the love of full clemency who received the ransomer gladly. We did not have inhuman masters, judges: they were such as could have been softened even by prayer; if tears had made up for a lack of gold, he would have brought both back at one time: he has testified that he did not want to happen what he did not pray for at great cost. Weigh, I beg you, what he may rightfully demand of me who did not help me in my extremity even by supplication. You added that you are protected by the privileges of nature and that what you did wrong against me may not be punished; but he does not have the prerogative of innocence who places his defence in rank. Let the guiltless shine by the light of his conduct: he confesses his crimes without pretence who reckons his protection lies in this, that he takes precedence: no authority defends the guilty: in criminals the sacred obligations of a name vanish.
EPILOGUE.

And this, most holy judges, after the guards of the robbers, I have pleaded with another labour of the heart, as if, even if I were not a debtor, I were able to provide what is demanded. He does not consider my bones stripped of flesh, filthy from the inhumanity of my masters, and he does not look at the secrets of nature laid open by the torturers. In my body the torments brought to light whatever a man is, and the inner recesses of my entrails were laid bare while the barbarian pressed on with tortures, when my father disdained to stand by me. Cruelty passes all measure which, even in exacting debts, does not first enquire into one's strength. When you see the vigour of youth in me softened by a load of miseries, when you see the strength of my years worn down by a variety of manifold calamities, when I have both the needs of old age and the resentment owed to youth, you do not cease to demand of me what even an enemy would have remitted to one exhausted. You will receive a tributary payment, and still you assail me with the greatness of the name and the guardian spirit of a parent, while you scorn to show even to your own child the compassion you owe to any man. May heavenly dispensation enrich your purpose with this reward: that you again look upon the longed-for funeral of your offspring, and that you, who are burdened by a living presence, may take the sum of your desires from tombs.
SPEECH XXII.
PREFACE.

The excellent young man has indeed arranged in order the riches of his inventions copiously, and has also endowed them with an abundance of words, and what he believed to be on the side of religion he has brought forth with a mouth worthy of reverence. But let the fabrications of malicious discourses keep far away, with their snares against reputation. We do not set the breast of our speech against Arator, nor do we cut down with a hostile pruning-hook the shoot of praise bursting into the light. Rather, in showing him what path of words he ought to follow, we know that we shall triumph more brilliantly in him if it falls out that he is preferred, because he drew from our store whatever, with God increasing it, he has lavishly poured out from the wealth of his knowledge.
THEME. LAW.
From a captured city of the enemy, priests and Vestal virgins are to be released free.

After a favourable outcome of the contest of war, amid triumphs and laurels, a law recited to the victors in order to resist them can have no force. What did we achieve with our swords through a love of death, if there is to be something for us to fear after battles? Whatever threatened us until now lies lifeless before my eyes, and now that the enemy's onset has been routed, I do not know what terror the decrees of dead emperors bring us. He does not know how to weigh the quality of proven valour who prides himself on a curb of papers for armed men. Let sluggish hearts acquiesce in these bars: I have scattered with the sword whatever took my licence from me. Anyone can deny us only what we do not want: I am content to have that boundary which my desires have not called me to cross. The law grants me to hold whatever I have prevailed over. Let leisure and the toga carry some weight with their denials: nature has given birth to the whole of whatever I wrest from the enemy while standing in battle array as mine. The only written law for us is to fear nothing. And these things indeed I have asserted to your ears as though the formula set against us were a good one. Yet the law, nurse of brave men, avenger of liberty, bulwark of the fatherland, bids its heroes, after the contest, take up the struggle again over their reward, and, not content with successful deeds, while it takes away the price of their sweat, it breaks their zeal for fighting. Are those precepts good, then, which come in the way to stop us from becoming good? Whatever laws take away the fruit of labours, most prudent censors, punish us on behalf of another's property. Is it fair that sanctions drawn up from a foreign law should have force? Or does it seem close to reason to cut off the hope of future possession? Why do you set against us the name of religion in the persons of priests? With God as my leader, whom you venerate in them, I prevailed. You, who wish them to escape the yoke of our servitude out of regard for him, should know that they are held captive at his own command. He strives against the gods who raises up those whom their sentence lays low: those whom you hasten to rescue would never have been made [the captives] of men, if they had deserved to be ministers of the heavenly ones. See, I am disputing with you about the savour of the law, as if I had no weapons to throw by way of reply. What justice do you think there is in that command which, to prop up the enemy, hands over the comrades who extended the empire? Take away the hope of plunder, and you have taken away the vows of combat. And if the guardian spirit of the laurelled victor is defrauded, whatever I sought in contempt of the light of life will turn to regret. Far be it from prudent men to seek fairness of this kind in what I will not call a law but a tyrant's inscription, which, displeasing to the divine powers, hostile to valour, fights against right and justice under a false colour of piety. You do not know, most talkative of men, how just a grief is born from the lost fruit of labour. This is to say: 'Whatever you have acquired with the gods as leaders, we snatch away.' I saw the enemy city growing old, as it were, in a single fire, and the very seats of the heaven-dwellers, deserted and stripped of divinity, laid low: and do you think anything remained that ought not to belong to the victor? What of the fact that this frivolous and empty enactment is itself confounded by obscurity? For it says that priests or Vestal virgins ought to enjoy freedom. I believe it names those in whom the dweller in heaven has shown his abode to be, whom heavenly favour has marked with its light as greater than men. The divine powers proclaim reverence for those priests whom they wish to be recognised. We saw the wretches whom [the law] protects, among the ashes of the fallen city, expecting help from lamentation alone, and, with no confidence in their calling, wandering among the crowds crushed by captivity. There was no unearthly splendour in their faces, no cheerfulness that would announce their office. Those for whom, in the storms of the world, a harbour presents itself in an innocent conscience do not know how to be troubled amid adversity. We saw more afflicted than the other trembling people those to whom you grant bare names, a laughable law. What place remains for merit, if that sacred office consists in a title alone? I believe it is one thing to be called [...], another to be a priest. I have often seen weapons aimed at the throat fall before faces worn by fasting, and swords blunted by unarmed men lose their rigid nature. If you will believe one about to speak of religion, he was no minister of temples who in any danger whatever needs human help. The supreme judge knows how to clothe his possession with light. That heavenly mingling is not hidden, and though it be clothed in the tunic of human frailty, it flashes forth. What of the fact that those who do not deserve to be dragged into servitude come of their own accord, ready to serve? He who is unworthy does not rebel against this extremity. Those come forward to obedience whose mind is worthy of the heights, and those whom it is sin to constrain to dishonour cast off the stubbornness of mortality. These men of yours, if they in no way deserve to be released, threaten dangers. Those cannot be withdrawn from men whom we do not perceive to have anything more than a man has. Help me, comrades, help me, partners, and with truth's aid suppress the garrulity of my opponent. A matter is at stake on which we already know what the judgement of the gods has thought. Let the undeserving be assigned [to us], so that we may have good priests. Let [priests] be established through those [gods] whom no conciliating tale, no uncertain defence, but the very radiance of the highest god proclaims to be his own.
SPEECH XXIII [AGAINST A DISOWNED SON WHO, HAVING KILLED HIS FATHER, ALSO PLOTTED AGAINST HIS MOTHER].

After the disowned son, judges, carrying out a grief he calls just, avenged with the sword his father's act and his mother's consent, he reckons he can disturb the innocence of the judges and filch something towards acquittal for a manifest crime. We do not know what commendatory words the criminal can find in his own defence, when for his refutation we show you the wound. The son, ruined by the evil of perseverance, after he killed his father, strives to extinguish his mother's reputation: grieving that we escaped the dagger, he pursues with a weapon our good name, for which, out of the modesty of our sex, we fear more. We show the father's severed neck, we show the criminal's path. He composes words against the facts and, so that no faithful support might seem to have remained to us, he has drawn our little one over to his view, whom, ignorant of deceit, he has subverted by a crafted art of words, making him too perish who was thought to be left to us. Why do you wish to veil naked justice with trickery? A hated man could not have spared, nor one whom you falsely say he loved have struck. Is there need of arguments where truth testifies to its deed with its own voice? You lost the hope of defence when you were scoring your mother's limbs with the sword. But although your advocate is handsome and polished, we have no eyes for looking at such things.
SPEECH XXIV, EXTEMPORE, WHICH DEUTERIUS HIMSELF SET.
THEME.
Having come safe through the sea, Diomedes, secure on dry land,
laments a shipwreck that happened without water.
She whom he had won by struggling through the various surges,
his wife, had passed into union with another.
The cause of complaint is real, though the name is feigned.
Attend his words, I pray, and be kind.
ADDRESS.

O divine powers, if not all things come about as you arrange them, your power is divided, or else you are the authors even of evils. But if care for human affairs troubles any one of your number, grant me either the happiness of one returning or the wandering which you ungratefully brought to an end. If heaven is to be called the possession of the pious, if what is prayed for is granted to mortals for moments of joy, do not join vengeance to your benefits. Why did we strain our vows towards fulfilment in such a way? So that, by the vote of the heavenly ones, adversity might be prepared out of the occasion of prosperity? Give back, I beg you, in your kindness, the hardships you took away: let the sea be restored, lest my reputation perish in a shipwreck on land. Next to good fortune is not knowing whatever evils have come. The disgrace that struck me to my face would not have touched me while absent. I would not be believed (oh, the outrage!) to have lost my wife, had I not returned to her: a calamity I had forsworn has overturned my state. The wandering on the liquid element was nearer to a safe anchorage: on my native soil I have lost the harbour which I often found in the bays of the vast deep. Is this the longed-for home, through desire for which forgetfulness of dangers was promised, when, in the hope of joy to come, the present shape of greater evils could be unknown? To whom have beginnings ever been born from the ends of miseries, or a fresh start come from misfortunes already gone through? Has it ever happened that what was longed for was not loved when obtained? Or has it come about that escape from danger harmed a man? Fortune, the worst of things, has always struck me with new blows: if her change tends to the worse, let her keep to a single form of harming, lest she grow insolent through successions. I had a wife, O companions of my ills, brought to chastity by the light of nature, in whom the splendour of her birth had grown through her upbringing, so that, defended by a twofold bulwark, she would by no means be believed to lie open to the blows of crimes, nor to soften the hardness of chastity by the disembowelling of obscenity. She never sought the tawny adornment of metal, nor imitated the snow of her body with the whiteness of precious stones; she had no aids to beauty while she pleased; she knew that the rights of the marriage bond are not helped by cosmetic efforts, and that a wife has not kept her husband bound when, once married, she has sought any splendour besides that which comes from character. The free servitude of raising her children kept her, while she showed herself such as deserved to be longed for and never thought her husband absent. She had hardened her sex with firmness of mind, while in her the weak counsels of a woman had taken substance from manly authority. She already resisted the lapses of her sex with teaching as her medicine, and laughed at the excesses of women carried over to other uses. In sum, she perished as one of those such as are wont to win tears from their husbands. By a Circaean cup, as they say, she was changed from herself and passed over into the desire of an adulterer. But what are we to do, caught amid anxieties and uncertainties? Let hated sailing receive us as a remedy, and let hands wearied by ropes once more take thought for bonds of tow: let my right hand cling to the tiller, to govern the laws of the bridled ship through the rudder; let the sky painted with stars be restored to my sight; let the routes of my plans be directed by the signs of the nights. Let it be a solace to my eyes if the land of a profaned marriage is not seen; let us flee the fatherland in which our marriage has been made such that it shames us to have lost it, and our prayers do not want to recover it.
25. SPEECH. THE WORDS OF THETIS WHEN SHE SAW ACHILLES DEAD.

The mother's deceit, devised by a loving plan, has been cut short. The fates have found our Achilles, though he was stolen away into another nature, and it did no good that cunning changed the sex his birth had given him. He did not learn to be a woman through length of time, and soft habit preserved the spirit of a brave man. Who would believe that a precaution devised by one who was both goddess and mother had no effect? Immortality is no reward when a mother does not pass it on to her offspring, and it offers no means of stealing a son away from misfortune. Are we deities only so that we may never be withdrawn from griefs? What sort of condition is this, when from the inmost depths of our womb we bring forth what is bound to death? The power of the heaven-dwellers ought either to be allowed to confer on its descendants what it possesses, or, when dear ones fall, to be granted death as an end to lamentation. We are lower than humans, whose like we bear, lying worse exposed to the mockery of the Parcae in this: that, though bound to our children, we cannot know death. Greatest of the gods, either withdraw our offspring from the hazards of chance, or subject us to them in return for the favour you have conferred. If we do not prevail, let it at least be allowed us to undergo death for one who is dear. Bereavement stands before my eyes, all the worse because, through the loftiness of my eternity, I knew it in advance. O lamentable happiness of the gods, when what cannot be unknown of adversity is not given to them to avert! I remember the anxiety of time past, and I recall my cares, over which I kept watch in vain. What use was it that my son's body was armed with the aid of the Stygian marsh, when we sought from a flood what he ought to have received from us? In the limbs of our child there is a place for a wound, the place the goddess held. Why did the water not mingle with looser fingers, so that the wave, mightier than the gods above, might have shut out blows entirely? And what help was it to have chosen Chiron's teaching, to make firm with instruction the slipperiness of youth? I believe we found, by the various paths of his training, that war would please my son: it came about with that most valiant tutor that the strength which followed did not follow our plans. Who would want a man who was to be hidden among the retreats of women to drink in the taste of combat, and so provide for a child by the very means through which he makes his provision perish? Already we were breaking at the wool-baskets hands hardened by spears, and a robe set off with gold or purple enclosed those shoulders which the hide of a flayed lion had warmed. It was no easy change for our young man to imitate a girl after he had tasted glory, and what I did not command in the first beginnings of tender age is not cunningly arranged. But why do I go over what is done, when the enormity of a calamity to come beats upon my mind? I see the destruction of smoking Troy, and see it overthrown while it still stands; I see the battles of Hector, bitter to the Greeks, who grew in repute for this reason, that by falling he might add to the worth of my son's triumph. I recognise the body, dragged by a four-horse chariot, of one who would still fight on, and that my Achilles' gain is lessened by whatever the dead man's weight loses; I see that to perish by a quick death profits [his] wrath. But why do I feed on these praises, I who am to be bereaved? The rest I shall cover in silence, so as not to be worn out by the telling before the time of grief. Let our eternity have from silence the consolation which it does not have from nature.
26. SPEECH. THE WORDS OF MENELAUS WHEN HE SAW TROY BURNED.

Although the ravisher inflamed my grief with heavy fires, although we endured the torches of injury, yet at the due time the author of the monstrous crime has been consumed on a pyre together with the whole community joined to him. An insult that earns such a vengeance, even with the greatest toil, is almost a happy one. Who would refuse to take up a necessity that is to close with the end of a triumph? The savour of what follows shuts out the bitterness of what went before: what we grieved over grows sweet, because those who provoked our grief repent of it. The occasion of a woman shamefully carried off became the mother of our increase: the wife separated from us has given birth to an empire, and out of the adulterer's embraces has brought forth for us the fatherland which we hold. Let those who laughed at me as a wifeless man see me trampling the proud necks of the enemy. We had a wife formed over a long time in honourable ways, ignorant of any other's bed, who would not wish to desire what is not permitted. Habit did not hurl her into vice; rather, at the impulse of a wicked robber, she followed Paris with a captive will. Never did awareness of her beauty raise her to the point of believing herself loved, for, as we are confident, those women are basest in character who keep in mind that they are beautiful. Such a vengeance befitted one who sinned greatly: he who took for himself the eminence of a revered wife has fallen utterly. Enjoy such a wedding, adulterer. With these emblems Alecto attends you as bridal attendant, and to be appeased [...]. So it was fitting that Paris too should perish so. We have dictated the laws of marriage not with words but with swords, laying waste the crop of presumption with an avenging sickle. Our having lost a marriage will serve many for its preservation. Tell me, you who anywhere have received the name of wife, will not the name and the courage of Menelaus come to mind whenever vices steal upon you? Those for whom chastity is not a matter of zeal will, unless we are mistaken, have it as a matter of necessity: an equal discipline will be kept by all, when both the willing and the compelled preserve one pattern.
27. SPEECH. THE WORDS OF JUNO WHEN SHE SAW THAT ANTAEUS HAD PROVED EQUAL TO THE STRENGTH OF HERCULES.

At long last someone has been found to answer to our judgement, someone to triumph over our enemy even while he is being defeated. Unless Hercules' strength crushes him, he will not stay down: the one we have provided is proud even of his falls. He stands great in his own strength, but he will be greatest through his overthrow. I do not know whether Hercules can be his equal, or whether Antaeus cannot by any means be laid low; but if adversity flatters our enemy, we have reached the laurels. We know what is to come, but it is fitting for the gods above to speak to mortals as if of human things. Let Hercules consider what he chooses must be done. He is to be beaten while his enemy engages him, and beaten too while his enemy lies on the ground. He who made sport of poisons in the cradle, who pacified the woods of Erymanthus, who outran the hind in speed, let him have the choice of what to pursue: either he will throw down his foe and so perish, or, if he fears the contest, he will already be buried along with his caution. A Lernaean peril, unless I am mistaken, will arise from the finishing of the contest. Who would not believe that nothing remains for him to accomplish, when his enemy is seen stretched on the ground? But the effort of our side will be roused by being crushed, and the very thing done against the enemy will happily supply a cause for increasing his strength.
28. SPEECH. [THE WORDS OF DIDO WHEN SHE SAW AENEAS DEPARTING.]
Neither was a goddess the parent of your race, nor Dardanus its founder.

As your harshness shows, you have lost the evidence of your birth, which you falsely claim by repute. It is plain that one who loves nothing is not the son of Venus: it is the order of things that character announces lineage, and that each follows the deeds of the one by whom he came into the light. The goddess of Idalium does not acknowledge one who does not know how to repay kindnesses. It is not report that shows who are sons, but likeness of conduct: if the disposition is different, the one called offspring can hardly be believed to be so. Rather, the crags of Caucasian harshness bore you, or a stony womb poured you out, conceived in the recesses of the mountains, and, lest your dreadful nature should be softened by nursing, Hyrcanian tigers, which rob others of life, gave you nourishment: you were reared by that savagery which slaughters. For why do I make myself promises by pretending? Or why am I held in suspense by hoping for better things? He did not give back tears for the weeping which I poured out, tormented by love of him; his bloody heart did not comfort my groans with sighs of its own. In my sorrows he did not offer himself as a companion with equal sorrow, which is the one remedy, since almost the only end to anguish is to have found someone to share it. But what

I am to say I do not know, nor do I know what to leave unsaid. Neither the favouring eye of Juno nor the gaze of the highest Thunderer will suffer this: that in return for so much spent I should be consumed by separation, and should have gained nothing by my devotion except to deserve not to be loved. Alas, faith driven out by all mortals, and that which until now joined men to the gods expelled! I, pitiable, took in a shipwrecked man and placed a queen under his rule, a captive while her good fortune still remained; I made the fugitive play master over the one who ruled. Now I am tormented, burning with fury, and I lament that my possessor deserts me. So you go away summoned by the auguries of Apollo, and you set the chance of a Lycian oracle above a sure realm already abiding with you? No doubt this cruelty is procured with the heavenly ones as its authors, and the interpreter of the gods drives a man to such excesses that he flees the shores of one who loves him as if hostile ground, that he who flees only affection betrays his safety amid storms. Go, I shall not delay you further. The road by which I am deserted holds my vengeance; the sea in its fury will hold judgement. I shall hear the hoarse surges of swelling gales: amid the dangers you will call the name of Dido, who both was a harbour and offered one; or surely, as I fear, lest while I am avenged you die while I still live, may I learn the outcome of the voyage you longed for after I have done with the light. See a reward not owed to crimes: I wish to perish innocent rather than see him perish deserving it.

Hard and untamed, he boasts that he sprang from the seed of Venus, and, disowning her, praises the goddess's lineage. So Venus bore one who flees the name of love, and the mercy of a raging heart poured out venom.
